objectives: Identify Egypt, Pharaoh and the Children of Israel and say one true fact about each.
Explain the chain fear → unfair treatment with a sentence from the chapter.
Discover when the chapter uses was or were, why it says “did not believe” (not *did not believed), and how “Because of + noun” gives a reason.
Name one fair way to use power, as your own idea.
content.pedagogy: Start with people, not grammar. Pairs build a two-column “who’s who” chart (Pharaoh / the Children of Israel) and copy each line from the text. The grammar grows out of the chart: You ask “One person or a group?” and learners see that the chart itself explains was and were. Keep “He thought he was a god” labelled as Pharaoh’s belief, and confirm each rule only after pairs have said it in their own words.
priorKnowledge: Present be (is / are), the simple past of regular verbs, the words king and group.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “He thought he was a god” is Pharaoh’s belief; the story says he did not believe in Allah and was an unfair and cruel ruler.
Pharaoh was not afraid of one person: He feared that “this crowd might take control of his kingdom”.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: was / were (one person / more than one) · believed in · did not + base verb (did not believe, did not think) · Because of + noun for a reason.
Notice (Activity 1): board “Pharaoh was the king of Egypt.” and “The Children of Israel were the children of Jacob (pbuh).”. Ask only: “One person or a group? Which word changes?” Pairs say the rule (one → was, a group → were) before you confirm it.
Build (Activities 2–3): fix “He did not believed” and “they did not thought” (did already shows the past), then build “Because of his fear, he was rude to the Children of Israel.” Ask: “What is the reason? What is the result?”
Likely errors: *They was · *did not believed · *Because his fear, … · *believed to Allah.
Use (Activity 4): three or four sentences about two people or groups in a school situation, with was and were, one did not + verb and one Because of + noun.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Chunk the reason sentence: “beCAUSE of his FEAR, | he was RUDE | to the CHILdren of ISrael.”
Weak forms: was /wəz/ and were /wə/ are short and quick: “PHARaoh was the KING of EGypt”, “they were the GRANDchildren …”.
In “he did not beLIEVE”, stress the main verb, not did.
Word focus: PHA-raoh (/ˈfeə.rəʊ/), MES-sen-ger, CRU-el, RU-ler, KING-dom, DAN-ger-ous.
beforeReading: Show the chapter picture and write “a cruel king”. Pairs say one thing a cruel king might do and one thing a fair king might do. Keep both lists on the board as predictions.
duringReading: First listening, books closed: Who are the two groups in the chapter?
Who’s-who chart: Pharaoh (was …, did not …, thought …) / the Children of Israel (were …, believed …), every line copied from the text.
Underline the “Because of” sentence and draw an arrow from the reason to the result.
Circle the three things Pharaoh did to the Children of Israel.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the chart in view.
Language Focus: Look (Activity 1: was / were / believed), Practise (Activity 2: did not + base verb, Activity 3: build the Because of sentence), Use (Activity 4).
Say, then write, three or four sentences about two people or groups and one reason.
Name one fair action a leader could choose instead, as your own idea.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: Chapter picture and “a cruel king”, pairs name one cruel and one fair action; 5–12 Listen with books closed (who are the two groups?), then listen and read along; 12–19 Who’s-who chart in pairs, every line copied from the text, quick whole-class check of the three unfair actions; 19–23 Quick Challenge individually; 23–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (one person or a group?), Activities 2–3 in pairs while you listen for “did not believed”; 31–38 Use: learners say, then write, three or four sentences about two teams or two classes (… was …, … were …, … did not …, Because of …), two pairs read aloud and the class names the reason; 38–40 Exit ticket
discussionPoints: Why was Pharaoh afraid of the Children of Israel?
Which three actions show that he treated them unfairly?
What could a powerful person do instead of treating a group unfairly? (your own idea)
interactiveTips: Use the Pharaoh hotspot for the left column of the chart and the Children of Israel hotspot for the right column.
Replay the last four sentences before Activity 3 so learners hear the reason and the result together.
When learners retell, keep “He thought he was a god” marked as Pharaoh’s belief.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the first words written: “Pharaoh was ____. He did not ____. The Children of Israel were ____. Because of his fear, ____.” Learners copy the missing words from the text before they write their own.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write five sentences comparing two groups in a school story using was, were, did not + verb and Because of, and underline the reason.

formativeAssessment: Names both groups and Pharaoh’s fear with evidence.
Chooses was / were correctly for one person and a group.
Uses did not + base verb and Because of + noun accurately.
expectedResponses: Pharaoh was the king of Egypt. He was unfair and cruel and did not believe in Allah. Because of his fear, he was rude to the Children of Israel and forced them to do dangerous work for no money.
content.transferTask: In two sentences, describe a fair way for a class president or team captain to use power, and say that it is your own idea.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners find the was / were rule from the chart before I named it, and did they keep Pharaoh’s belief separate from what the story says?

classroomManagement.instructions: Work with your partner. Make a who’s-who chart: Pharaoh, the Egyptians, the Children of Israel. Copy every line from the story.
checkQuestions: Do you write your own words? (no, words from the story)
How many unfair actions do we check together? (three)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Listen in Activities 2–3 for “did not believed” and give the base verb quietly. Check that pairs find Pharaoh’s fear as the reason. Ask the class to name the reason after the two Use readings.

exitTicket: Complete: “Pharaoh ____ the king of Egypt. He did not ____ in Allah. Because of his ____, he was rude to the Children of Israel.”

rubricLevels.secure: Names Pharaoh’s fear and how he treated the Children of Israel, with evidence.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the sentence with “Because of his fear”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses was for one person and were for a group.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “One person or a group?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses did not + base verb.
rubricLevels.notYet: Write “did not believed / did not believe” and ask which is right.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses Because of + a reason.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “Because of …, he …”.

interculturalFocus.notice: The story begins in ancient Egypt with a king called Pharaoh and the Children of Israel, a group of people who lived there.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: What do you know about Egypt today (Cairo, the Nile, the pyramids)? Which Turkish names are used for these people (Firavun, İsrailoğulları) and which English ones (Pharaoh, the Children of Israel)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: The chapter speaks about one cruel ruler, not about Egyptians today. Learners do not use the story to judge any nation.

objectives: Put the events in order: dream → helpers and magicians → the king’s order → the soldiers’ action.
Separate what the magicians said would happen from what the story says happened.
Discover that some past verbs change their form (had, saw, came, found, told), that will + base verb talks about the future, and how One day / Then / When order the events.
Talk about injustice calmly, without detail.
content.pedagogy: This chapter is sensitive: Read the last paragraph once, calmly, and never act it out. The main task is order and voice: Learners put event cards in order and mark who says each sentence (the narrator, the magicians, the king). The grammar comes from that order: “Did the dream happen already? Then why no -ed?” and “The magicians talk about when — before or after?” lead learners to irregular past forms and will.
priorKnowledge: Regular past with -ed, first / then for order.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The magicians’ words (“A boy will be born … and he will kill the Egyptians”) are a prediction, not something the story says has happened.
The fire in the dream did not hurt any of the Children of Israel.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: irregular past verbs (had, saw, came, found, told) · past for the dream (burnt) vs will + base verb for the magicians’ prediction (will be born, will kill) · order with One day, Then and When + past.
Notice (Activity 1): learners find had, saw, came, found and told in the text and match them with have, see, come, find, tell. Ask: “Did these things happen already? Where is the -ed?” Learners say that some verbs change their whole form in the past.
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose burnt / will / will and ask “Is this the dream or the magicians talking about later?”, then order five sentences and circle One day, Then and When.
Likely errors: *The fire burns the houses (present in a past story) · *A boy will born · *he will kills · *When they find (present).
Use (Activity 4): a harmless new situation with one prediction (It will rain tomorrow), one safe instruction (Take your umbrella) and one When + past sentence.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Irregular pasts are short and clear: HAD, SAW, CAME, FOUND, TOLD. Regular -ed: called /d/, asked /t/, searched /t/, cried /d/.
will is weak: “a BOY will be BORN” (/wɪl/, often ’ll in fast speech).
Chunk the dream sentence: “the FIRE came from jeRUsalem | and BURNT the HOUses | of the eGYPtians.”
Word focus: de-SPOT-ic, ma-GI-cians (/dʒ/), HEART-less, SOL-diers (/dʒ/), je-RU-sa-lem, e-GYP-tians. Keep a calm, even voice in the last paragraph.
beforeReading: Set a calm reading rule: “Today we look at decisions and their results, not at violent details.” Then ask: “Can a dream be scary? What might a king do after a bad dream?” Keep answers as predictions.
duringReading: First listening: What did the king see in his dream?
Number five event cards while listening a second time.
Mark who speaks each quoted sentence: The magicians or the king.
Underline the time words One day, Then and When.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the event cards in order.
Language Focus: Look (Activity 1: irregular past verbs), Practise (Activity 2: past or will? Activity 3: order the events), Use (Activity 4).
Write three safe sentences: a prediction, an instruction and a When + past sentence.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Calm frame and hook: “What might a king do after a bad dream?”, two predictions on the board; 4–11 Listen with books closed (what did the king see?), then listen and read along, the teacher reads the last paragraph once, calmly; 11–18 Event cards in pairs: Order five cards, then mark each quote M (magicians) or K (king), whole-class check; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 as a pair race (find the five past verbs in the text first), Activities 2–3 in pairs with the question “Dream or prediction?”; 30–38 Use: Weather forecast game, one learner predicts (It will …), the partner gives a safe instruction (Take …), then both write one When + past sentence about yesterday; 38–40 Exit ticket
discussionPoints: What did the king see in his dream?
What did the magicians say would happen?
The king acted out of fear. What would have been a fair and responsible choice? (your own idea)
interactiveTips: Use the Fire in the Dream hotspot for the first paragraph and the A Cruel Order hotspot only to confirm the order of events.
Replay the magicians’ sentence and ask: “Is this a fact or a prediction?”
Do not act out, draw or discuss the violence in detail.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give five picture-free event cards with the verb underlined and the frame “One day, … Then, … When …, …”. For Activity 1, show the past verbs in the text first.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a five-sentence summary of the chapter using three irregular past verbs, one will-prediction marked as the magicians’ words, and Then.

formativeAssessment: Orders the events correctly.
Marks the magicians’ words as a prediction.
Uses irregular past forms and will + base verb accurately.
expectedResponses: The king had a dream about a fire from Jerusalem. The magicians said, “A boy will be born … and he will kill the Egyptians.” Then the king gave a cruel order to his soldiers. The soldiers were unkind and heartless.
content.transferTask: Give one example of a calm, responsible choice when you feel afraid of something that might happen.
content.teacherReflection: Did the lesson stay calm, and did learners separate the magicians’ prediction from the events in the story?

classroomManagement.instructions: With your partner, put the five event cards in order. Then mark each quote M for the magicians or K for the king.
checkQuestions: How many cards? (five)
What does M mean? (the magicians said it)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Read the last paragraph yourself once, calmly. Check that the magicians’ words are marked as a prediction. In the forecast game, listen for will + base verb and a safe instruction.

exitTicket: Write the past form: have → ____, see → ____, tell → ____. Then write one sentence with will about tomorrow.

rubricLevels.secure: Puts the events in order.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the first and last cards.

rubricLevels.secure: Says the magicians’ words are a prediction, not a fact.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Did it happen yet?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses irregular past verbs such as had, said and gave.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the base forms and let the learner find the past forms in the text.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses will + base verb.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “It will … tomorrow.”.

interculturalFocus.notice: The king's helpers and magicians explain his dream. People in many cultures have tried to explain dreams.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Do people in Türkiye talk about the meaning of dreams (rüya tabiri, 'Hayırdır inşallah')? What do English speakers say after a strange dream ('It was just a dream', 'Sweet dreams')?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners share only a phrase, not their own dreams. Respect families who take dreams seriously and those who do not.

content.chapter: Chapter 3 — A Baby in a Basket
objectives: Follow the chain problem → instructions → actions → feeling in the chapter.
Show that the mother did what she was told, with sentences from the text.

Discover the difference between could (a possible danger) and could not (not able), how instructions and a promise are made (Take …, Put …, will …), and how the chapter says told her daughter to follow and kinder than.
Explain trust through what the mother does.
content.pedagogy: Use a three-box story map: Problem / Instructions / Actions. Learners match each instruction with the action the mother really did, so trust becomes something they can see in the text. The grammar starts from the problem box: “Did the soldiers find the baby? Could the mother sleep?” helps learners discover the two meanings of could before you name them.
priorKnowledge: can / can’t for ability, imperatives in classroom language (Open your books.).
anticipatedMisconceptions: “soldiers could find her baby” does not mean they found him: It is the danger she was afraid of.
The mother was very worried and sad, but she knew that Allah was kinder to the baby than she was.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: could + base verb for a possible danger vs could not + base verb for “not able” · instructions with the base verb and will for a promise, noticed in Allah’s words (read, never gapped) · past forms that tell the story (put, took, carried) · told + person + to + base verb · kinder than.
Notice (Activity 1): “His mother was afraid that soldiers could find her baby. So, she could not sleep at night.” Ask: “Did the soldiers find the baby? Was she able to sleep?” Pairs say what could and could not mean here.
Build (Activities 2–3): Complete put / took / carried in the story sentences (Allah’s words themselves are only read and matched to the mother’s actions), then fix “told her daughter follow” and “more kind”.
Likely errors: *could not find (changes the danger) · *taked / *carryed · *told her daughter follow · *more kind than / *more kinder.
Use (Activity 4): a safe new situation with a difficulty (could not), an instruction and a promise (will), for example helping a younger child on the first day of school.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Instructions are short with a falling tune: “TAKE a BASket. | PUT your BAby in the BASket. | TAKE the BASket to the RIVer NILE.”
Stress NOT when it changes the meaning: “she could NOT SLEEP at NIGHT.”
-ed endings: carried /d/, worried /d/.
Word focus: BAS-ket, pro-TECT, WOR-ried, KIN-der, DAUGH-ter (/ˈdɔː.tə/, gh is silent).
beforeReading: Recall Chapter 2 in one sentence (the king’s order). Then ask: “What could a mother do to keep her baby safe?” Keep ideas as predictions.
duringReading: First listening: What was the mother afraid of?
Three boxes: Problem / Instructions / Actions, each line copied from the text.
Draw lines from each instruction to the action she did.
Underline the sentence with “kinder … than”.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Look (Activity 1: could / could not), Practise (Activity 2: what she did — put, took, carried, Activity 3: told her daughter to follow, kinder than), Use (Activity 4).
Write three or four sentences about helping someone in a difficult but safe situation.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: One-sentence recall of Chapter 2, then “What could a mother do to keep her baby safe?”; 4–11 Listen with books closed (what was she afraid of?), then listen and read along; 11–18 Story map in pairs: Problem / Instructions / Actions, then draw lines from each instruction to the action she did, whole-class check; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Did they find the baby? Could she sleep?), Activity 2 in pairs (past forms of the mother’s actions), Activity 3 in pairs; 30–38 Use: Pairs plan help for a worried younger child (He could not … . Take … . I will … . I told him to …), then say it to another pair; 38–40 Exit ticket
discussionPoints: What was the mother afraid of?
Which actions show that she did what she was told?
What does “Allah was kinder to the baby Moses than she was” tell us about her feelings?
interactiveTips: Use The Basket hotspot for the instructions and The River Nile hotspot for the water carrying the basket away.
Replay the instructions and ask learners to hold up one finger for each instruction they hear.
Let learners try the Quick Challenge before you reveal anything.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the story map with the instructions already written; learners copy the matching actions. Frames for Use: “He could not ____. Take ____. I will ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write five sentences about a safe difficulty using could not, one instruction, will, told … to … and one comparison with -er than.

formativeAssessment: Matches instructions with actions from the text.
Explains the difference between could and could not in the chapter.
Uses told + person + to + base verb and -er than correctly.
expectedResponses: The mother was afraid that soldiers could find her baby, so she could not sleep. She put the baby in a basket, took it to the river and told her daughter to follow the basket. She knew that Allah was kinder to the baby than she was.
content.transferTask: Describe one action that shows trust in a difficult but safe situation, for example the first day at a new school.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see trust in the mother’s actions, and did they discover the two meanings of could before I explained them?

classroomManagement.instructions: With your partner, make a story map: Problem, Instructions, Actions. Draw a line from each instruction to the action the mother did.
checkQuestions: What are the three parts? (problem, instructions, actions)
What do the lines connect? (an instruction and an action)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that “told her daughter to follow the basket” is linked to the right action. Listen for could and could not in Activity 1. In the Use task, check told + person + to.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “could not” and one with “told … to …” about your morning.

rubricLevels.secure: Matches the instructions with the actions from the text.
rubricLevels.notYet: Read one instruction and ask “What did she do?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains could and could not in the chapter.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Could she sleep?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses told + person + to + base verb.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “She told her daughter to …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses -er than correctly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give “kinder than” as a model.

interculturalFocus.notice: Moses's mother puts the baby in a basket on the river to save him. Rivers are at the heart of life in many lands.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which rivers are important in Türkiye (Fırat, Dicle, Kızılırmak)? Which river is important in Egypt (the Nile) and in London (the Thames)? What did people use rivers for in the past?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners compare the role of rivers, not which country is richer or more beautiful.

objectives: Follow the basket from the water to the palace and to Queen Asiye.
Describe Asiye with evidence and compare her with her husband.
Discover the difference between moving to a place (came to, took it to, ran to) and being in a place (near, nearby), use different from, and tell a decision (I will …) from an order (Find …).
Recognize the sister’s quick, helpful action.
content.pedagogy: Draw a simple route on the board: water → edge of the river → palace → the king and the queen, and let learners put the movement phrases from the text on the arrows. That route is the first Language Focus task: Learners notice that movement uses to while place uses near / nearby. Then build a character card for Asiye from actions, not only adjectives.
priorKnowledge: Simple adjectives (good, kind), will for the future, the imperative.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The palace servants took the basket to the king and the queen; the king accepted Asiye’s decision.
Moses’s sister did not say “She is my mother”; she said “I know a good woman … She will be a good nurse for the baby.”
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: movement verb + to (came to, took it to, ran to) vs place (near, nearby) · different from · I will + base verb for a decision · an order with the base verb (Find …).
Notice (Activity 1): pairs sort five parts of the chapter. Ask: “Is something moving? Where to? Or is it only telling us where something is?” Learners say: movement → to, place → near / nearby.
Build (Activities 2–3): Match different from, kind-hearted, accepted and placed with their meanings, then choose will / Find and ask “Is Asiye deciding or giving an order?”
Likely errors: *different than / *different of · *ran at the Queen · *I take him (no decision) · *Found a nurse (past instead of an order).
Use (Activity 4): a helpful plan for a new classmate (She is kind-hearted. She is different from … I will … Find …).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Contrastive stress: “The QUEEN was DIFferent from her HUSband.”
Decision: “I will TAKE him to the PALace | and LOOK after him.”
Order with a clear fall: “FIND a NURSE for the BAby.”
-ed endings: accepted /ɪd/, placed /t/.
Word focus: PAL-ace, kind-HEART-ed, SER-vants, WA-ter-side, ac-CEPT-ed, near-BY.
beforeReading: Ask: “Where was the basket at the end of Chapter 3?” Draw the river on the board and ask learners to predict where it will stop.
duringReading: First listening: Where did the basket stop?
Put the movement phrases from the text on the route arrows.
Find two actions that show Asiye’s care.
Underline the sister’s words.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Look (Activity 1: going somewhere or being somewhere?), Practise (Activity 2: words about the queen, Activity 3: decision or order?), Use (Activity 4).
Write a helpful plan for a new classmate in four sentences.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: River drawn on the board, “Where will the basket stop?”; 4–11 Listen with books closed (where did it stop?), then listen and read along; 11–18 Route on the board: Pairs write came to / took it to / ran to on the arrows and near / nearby next to the places, then a character card for Asiye with two actions from the text; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 checks the route, Activity 2 in pairs, Activity 3 as a quick “decision or order?” thumbs-up / thumbs-down round; 30–38 Use: Pairs write a plan to help a new classmate (… is kind-hearted, … is different from …, I will …, Find …), then read it to another pair; 38–40 Exit ticket
discussionPoints: How was Asiye different from her husband?
Which actions show her care for the baby?
How did Moses’s sister help?
interactiveTips: Use the Queen Asiye hotspot for the character card and The King’s Palace hotspot for the route.
Replay “I will take him …” and “Find a nurse …” one after the other and ask which one is a decision.
Keep answers to the actions in the text.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the route with blanks (came __ the edge of the river, took it __ the king) and the frames “She was different from ____.” and “I will ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write five sentences comparing two people you know with different from, one decision with I will and one order.

formativeAssessment: Separates movement phrases from place phrases.
Describes Asiye with an action from the text.
Uses different from and tells a decision from an order.
expectedResponses: The basket came to the edge of the river near the palace. Queen Asiye was different from her husband: She believed in Allah and was kind-hearted. She said, “I will take him to the palace and look after him,” and told her servants to find a nurse.
content.transferTask: Describe one useful action that shows care for a new classmate.
content.teacherReflection: Did the route help learners discover to vs near, and did they describe Asiye with actions, not only adjectives?

classroomManagement.instructions: Write came to, took it to and ran to on the arrows of the river on the board. Then write two actions of Asiye on her card.
checkQuestions: What goes on the arrows? (came to, took it to, ran to)
How many actions for Asiye? (two)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that near and nearby go next to places, not on arrows. In the thumbs round, watch for learners who mix a decision and an order. In the Use task, check different from.

exitTicket: Write one “different from” sentence and one decision with “I will …” about this week.

rubricLevels.secure: Separates movement phrases from place phrases.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Is it moving or is it a place?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Describes Asiye with an action from the text.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to “I will take him to the palace”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses different from correctly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “… is different from …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Tells a decision (I will) from an order (find).
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Is she deciding or telling someone?”.

interculturalFocus.notice: Queen Asiye loves the baby and takes care of him, even though her husband is cruel. In Turkish she is called Asiye; English writers may also call her Asiya.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Why does the same name change in different languages (Asiye / Asiya, Musa / Moses, Harun / Aaron)? Can you find your own name in another language?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners notice that good people can be found in every family and every palace. Asiye is a model of courage across cultures.

objectives: Explain how Moses came back to his mother and grew up in a safe place.
Say what did not change in Moses (always …) and give the reason for his love for the Children of Israel.

Discover that take care of / look after mean the same, that grew up / became show change over time, that because is followed by a subject + verb, and that “was walking … saw” shows an action in progress and a new event.
Connect helping the weak with a safe, concrete action.
content.pedagogy: Build a timeline rope across the board: baby → back to his mother → grew up → a strong young man → one day in the bazaar. Groups hold one time card each and stand in order. The last card leads to the Language Focus: “One day he was walking in the bazaar. He saw two men. They were fighting.” Which started first? Learners discover the background action and the new event from their own timeline.
priorKnowledge: because from earlier chapters, past simple, the idea of “always”.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Moses did not grow up in his mother’s house: He grew up “in a safe place, in the house of the king”.
“One day he was walking in the bazaar” describes the moment; the new event is that he saw two men.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: take care of / look after (same meaning) · grew up / became for change over time · always · because + subject + verb (not because of) · was + -ing for an action in progress + past simple for a new event (was walking … saw).
Notice (Activity 1): pairs match take care of, grew up, became, the weak people and bazaar with their meanings. Ask: “Which two phrases mean the same? Which two show a change over time?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Complete always / because and ask why it is not because of (a subject and a verb follow: his mother was …), then decide true or false: “Moses started walking after he saw the two men.”
Likely errors: *because of his mother was … · *became to a strong young man · *He was walk · *He walked in the bazaar when he was seeing ….
Use (Activity 4): three or four sentences about someone who helps others (looks after, became, always, because).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Linking: “LOOKED_afTER” (/lʊkt‿ɑːftə/), “GREW_UP”.
Chunk the background and the new event: “one DAY | he was WALKing in the baZAAR. | he SAW two MEN. | they were FIGHTing.”
-ed endings: looked /t/, loved /d/, passed /t/.
Word focus: pro-TEC-tor, ba-ZAAR, AL-ways, e-GYP-tian, READ-y.
beforeReading: Recall: Who offered to find a nurse in Chapter 4? Ask learners to predict who the nurse will be.
duringReading: First listening: Was the prediction right?
Write one time card per group: baby / back to his mother / grew up / strong young man / one day in the bazaar.
Underline always and because.
Box “he was walking” and “He saw”.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Look (Activity 1: care and change), Practise (Activity 2: always and because, Activity 3: walking, then seeing), Use (Activity 4).
Write three or four sentences about a helpful person in your life.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: “Who will be the nurse?” predictions; 4–11 Listen with books closed (was the prediction right?), then listen and read along; 11–19 Timeline rope: Five groups write one time card each with a sentence from the text, stand in order at the front, the class checks the order; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 in pairs, Activity 2 with the question “Why because and not because of?”, Activity 3 as whole-class discovery using the last two cards of the timeline; 31–38 Use: Learners describe a helpful person (He always … . She looks after … . He became … because …), rehearse with a partner, then write; 38–40 Exit ticket
discussionPoints: How did Moses come back to his mother?
Where did Moses grow up, and what did he always know?
Why did Moses love the Children of Israel?
interactiveTips: Use the His Mother’s Arms hotspot for the first half of the timeline and The Bazaar hotspot for the last card.
Replay “One day he was walking in the bazaar. He saw two men. They were fighting.” before Activity 3.
Keep helping the weak safe and concrete in the Use step.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the timeline cards with one word missing each and the frames “He always ____.” and “He loved ____ because ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write five sentences about someone who grew up and became something, with always, because and one was + -ing … when … sentence.

formativeAssessment: Orders the timeline correctly.
Uses because + subject + verb (not because of).
Explains which action was in progress and which was new.
expectedResponses: Moses’s sister brought her mother to the palace, and his mother looked after him. Moses grew up in the house of the king and became a strong young man. He loved the Children of Israel because his mother was from the Children of Israel.
content.transferTask: Describe one safe way to help someone younger or weaker at school.
content.teacherReflection: Did the timeline help learners discover the background action and the new event, and did helping stay concrete and safe?

classroomManagement.instructions: Each group writes one time card with a sentence from the story. Stand in order at the front. The class checks the order.
checkQuestions: How many cards does each group write? (one)
Who checks the order? (the class)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check the order of the time cards. In Activity 2, ask why because and not because of. In the Use task, listen for always and became.

exitTicket: Complete: “I was walking to school when I ____.” and “I always ____ because ____.”

rubricLevels.secure: Orders the timeline.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the first and last cards.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses care and change words: looked after, grew up, became.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to each phrase in the text.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses because + subject + verb, not because of.
rubricLevels.notYet: Write both and ask what follows each.

rubricLevels.secure: Says which action was in progress and which was new.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Was it happening already?”.

interculturalFocus.notice: Moses goes back to his mother and grows up safely in the palace, but he always knows his own people.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: What helps a child remember their family and roots when they grow up in a different place (language at home, food, stories)? Do you know a family who lives abroad and keeps Turkish customs?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners talk about keeping roots with respect for both cultures a child lives in.

content.chapter: Chapter 6 — A Mistake in the Bazaar
objectives: Keep the text’s distinction: Moses ran to help, and the death was accidental.
Follow the chain: Feeling sorry → dua → forgiveness → a man’s warning.
Discover what accidentally means, how to + verb gives a purpose and because gives a reason, and how the man separates now (are looking for you) from what he expects (are going to catch you).
Name a responsible next step after a mistake.
content.pedagogy: Handle the death in one calm sentence and move on to responsibility. A three-column chart does the work: What Moses wanted / What happened / What he did next. The word accidentally is the key to the chart, so the Language Focus starts there: “Did Moses plan this?” Then the man’s warning becomes a “now / soon” line on the board, which is where learners discover are looking and are going to.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The text says Moses accidentally caused a death: He ran to help, not to kill.
Moses’s dua is his own prayer; learners read it as it is and do not change it.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: accidentally = not on purpose · to + base verb for a purpose (ran to help him) · because + subject + verb for a reason (because He is Kind and Loving) · are + -ing for now (are looking for you) vs are going to + base verb for what the man expects (are going to catch you).
Notice (Activity 1): “He was so sorry because he accidentally caused someone’s death.” Ask: “Did Moses plan this? Which word tells us?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose to help / because and ask “Why did he run? Why did Allah forgive him?”, then fix “are look for” and “going catch” with the question “What is happening now? What does the man expect next?”
Likely errors: *ran for help him · *accidental caused · *are look for you · *are going catch you.
Use (Activity 4): a safe warning in a harmless situation (The bus is leaving. We are going to miss it. Run!).
content.pronunciationFocus:
ac-ci-DEN-tal-ly has five syllables: Do not drop “-tal-” (/ˌæk.sɪˈden.təl.i/).
Now vs soon: “they are LOOKing for you” / “they are GOing to CATCH you”; “going to” is weak (/ˈɡəʊ.ɪŋ tə/).
Moses’s dua is read slowly and calmly, exactly as written: “forGIVE me. | I acciDENtally CAUSED someone’s DEATH.”
-ed endings: shouted /ɪd/, caused /d/, killed /d/.
Word focus: up-SET, for-GIVE, WARN-ing, e-GYP-tian.
beforeReading: Set the reading rule: “Today we look at what someone wanted, what happened and what he did next.” Ask: “What should a person do after a big mistake?” Collect three ideas.
duringReading: First listening: Why did Moses run?
Three columns: What Moses wanted / What happened / What he did next, each with a quoted phrase.
Circle accidentally (twice).
Mark the man’s words: NOW (are looking) and SOON (are going to).
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Look (Activity 1: accidentally), Practise (Activity 2: to help / because, Activity 3: the man’s warning), Use (Activity 4).
Write a safe warning for an everyday situation and one responsible next step after a small mistake.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Frame and hook: “What should a person do after a big mistake?”, three ideas on the board; 4–10 Listen with books closed (why did Moses run?), then listen and read along calmly; 10–18 Three-column chart in pairs (wanted / happened / did next), whole-class check that accidentally is in the middle column; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Did he plan it?), Activities 2–3 in pairs, then a “now / soon” line on the board with the man’s two sentences; 30–38 Use: Pairs write a safe warning (The bus is leaving now. We are going to miss it. Run!) and one responsible step after a small mistake (I broke …, so I …), two pairs read aloud; 38–40 Exit ticket
discussionPoints: Why did Moses run to the two men?
Which word shows that Moses did not plan the result?
What did Moses do after the mistake, and what can a person do after a mistake at school?
interactiveTips: Use the Not on Purpose hotspot for the first half of the chart and The Warning hotspot for the man’s words.
Replay the man’s words and ask learners to raise one hand for “now” and two hands for “soon”.
Do not act out or draw the fight.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the column heads and the first words: “He ran to ____. It was not on ____. He asked Allah ____.” Frames for Use: “____ is ____-ing now. We are going to ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write five sentences about a small, safe mistake: what you wanted (to …), what happened (accidentally), why you were sorry (because …) and what you did next.

formativeAssessment: Keeps purpose and accidental result apart.
Uses to + verb for purpose and because for a reason.
Separates are + -ing (now) from are going to (expected).
expectedResponses: Moses ran to help the man from the Children of Israel. The Egyptian died, but Moses did not plan it: He accidentally caused his death. He was very sorry and asked Allah to forgive him, and Allah forgave him. A man from the city warned him to run away.
content.transferTask: Describe a small, safe mistake and one responsible next step.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners keep “accidentally” as the story says, and did the lesson move calmly from the event to responsibility?

classroomManagement.instructions: With your partner, make three columns: what Moses wanted, what happened, what he did next.
checkQuestions: How many columns? (three)
Where does “accidentally” go? (in the middle column)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Keep the tone calm. Check that pairs keep purpose and accidental result apart. Listen for are going to in the warning. In the Use task, check that the step after the mistake is responsible.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “accidentally” and one with “are going to” about a safe everyday situation.

rubricLevels.secure: Keeps what he wanted and what happened by accident apart.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Did he plan it?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses to + verb for purpose and because for a reason.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give one model of each.

rubricLevels.secure: Separates are + -ing (now) and are going to (soon).
rubricLevels.notYet: Draw the now and soon line.

rubricLevels.secure: Says one responsible step after a small mistake.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “I broke …, so I …”.

interculturalFocus.notice: Moses tries to help someone in the bazaar, and a man is killed by accident. Markets are busy, crowded places in every culture.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: What is a bazaar or market like in your town (Konya Bedesten, a weekly pazar)? Which English words describe a market (stall, seller, customer, crowded)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: This chapter includes an accident. Keep the comparison to market life, not to violence.

objectives: Follow the journey: Egypt → a long journey → Midian → the well.
Explain why Moses looked for water and describe the scene at the well.
Discover that there were tells us what was in a place, were + -ing tells us what people were doing, and use arrived at, So and look for.
Notice that the two girls did not go near the well.
content.pedagogy: Use a picture dictation: The teacher reads the well scene twice and learners sketch it (the well, many men with their sheep, two girls far from the water; nobody draws Moses). Then they check the sketch against the text. The sketch leads straight into the Language Focus: “What is there? What are the people doing?” lets learners discover there were and were + -ing themselves.
priorKnowledge: there is / there are, present continuous, simple past journey verbs (went, left).
anticipatedMisconceptions: The text says only that Midian was near Egypt and that the king of Egypt was not the ruler there; do not add other geography.
Moses was not alone: “Allah guided him.”
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: There were + plural noun (what was in a place) · were + -ing for a scene (were watering, were sitting) · arrived at + place · So for a result · look for (= try to find).
Notice (Activity 1): “There were many men around the water. They were watering their animals.” Ask: “Which sentence tells us what was at the well? Which tells us what the people were doing?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Complete at / So / for (Why do we say arrive at, not arrive to?), then match escaped from, guided, thirsty, a well and shepherds with their meanings.
Likely errors: *There was many men · *They was watering · *arrived to Midian · *looked water.
Use (Activity 4): Describe arriving somewhere familiar (the canteen, a park): After …, we arrived at … There were … They were …-ing.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Weak forms in the scene: “there were” (/ðə wə/), “they were WAtering”.
Chunk the result: “MOses was TIRED and THIRSty, | SO he LOOKED for WAter.”
-ed endings: escaped /t/, traveled /d/, guided /ɪd/, arrived /d/, looked /t/.
Word focus: MID-i-an, SHEP-herds (/ˈʃep.ədz/, the h is silent), THIRS-ty, es-CAPED, GUID-ed.
beforeReading: Recall the man’s warning from Chapter 6. Ask: “Where can Moses go? What will he need on a long journey?” Collect ideas (water, food, rest).
duringReading: First listening: Where did Moses arrive?
Picture dictation: The teacher reads the scene at the well twice, learners sketch it (no drawing of Moses).
Check the sketch: underline “There were” and every “were + -ing”.
Find the sentence that shows why Moses looked for water.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Look (Activity 1: at the well), Practise (Activity 2: arriving and looking, Activity 3: journey words), Use (Activity 4).
Describe arriving at a familiar place in four sentences.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: “What will Moses need on a long journey?” ideas on the board; 4–10 Listen with books closed (where did he arrive?), then listen and read along; 10–18 Picture dictation: The teacher reads the well scene twice, learners sketch it, then pairs check the sketch against the text and add labels from it; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery with the sketches (what is there? what are they doing?), Activities 2–3 in pairs; 30–38 Use: Learners describe arriving at a familiar place (After …, we arrived at … . There were … . They were …-ing.), rehearse in pairs, then write; 38–40 Exit ticket
discussionPoints: Why did Moses leave Egypt?
Why did he look for water?
What were the shepherds doing, and where were the two girls?
interactiveTips: Use the Midian hotspot for the journey and The Well hotspot to check the sketches.
Replay the well scene before Activity 1.
Accept only place information that is in the text.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a half-drawn scene with labels to copy from the text and the frames “There were ____. They were ____-ing.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write five sentences about arriving somewhere with After …, arrived at, So …, There were … and two were + -ing actions.

formativeAssessment: Orders the journey correctly.
Uses There were for what was in a place and were + -ing for actions.
Uses arrived at and looked for correctly.
expectedResponses: Moses escaped from the soldiers and arrived at Midian. He was tired and thirsty, so he looked for water. At the well there were many shepherds. They were watering their animals. Two girls were sitting far from the water.
content.transferTask: Describe arriving at a familiar place and what people were doing there.
content.teacherReflection: Did the sketches help learners discover the two jobs (what is there / what people were doing), and did they keep to the place information in the text?

classroomManagement.instructions: Listen as I read the well scene twice. Draw it. Then check your drawing with your partner against the story and add labels.
checkQuestions: How many times do I read? (twice)
What do you add after the check? (labels from the story)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Do not draw Moses. Check that the drawings show the shepherds watering and the two girls far from the water. In Activity 1, use the drawings to ask what is there and what people are doing.

exitTicket: Write two sentences about your classroom this morning: One with “There were …” and one with “… were …-ing”.

rubricLevels.secure: Orders the journey.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the places on cards.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses There were for things in a place and were + -ing for actions.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the drawing and ask “What was there? What were they doing?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses arrived at and looked for correctly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “He arrived at …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Says why he looked for water with evidence.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “How did he feel?”.

interculturalFocus.notice: Moses travels from Egypt to Midian, a land east of Egypt, and arrives at a well. In the desert the well is the meeting place.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Where do people meet in a Turkish village or town (the çeşme, the kahvehane, the mosque courtyard)? Where do people meet in an English village (the pub, the church hall, the village green)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Meeting places differ by culture and religion. Learners describe them without judging.

objectives: Explain why the sisters waited far from the well.
Describe how Moses helped and what changed for the sisters.
Discover what cannot tells us, where aren’t goes in a Why question, and use there are no + plural noun and wait for + person + to + verb.
Connect helpfulness with a real need.
content.pedagogy: Problem → need → help. Pairs build a problem-solution chain from the sisters’ words: Our father is very old → He cannot come → There are no young men → We wait for our turn → Moses helped → They came home early. The chain gives the context for each Language Focus item, so learners discover the meaning of cannot and the structure of the question from what they have just explained.
priorKnowledge: can / can’t, Why … ? questions, present continuous.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “He cannot come with us” means their father is not able because he is very old; it does not mean he does not want to.
The sisters came home early because they did not wait for the other shepherds to leave the well.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: cannot + base verb (not able) · Why + aren’t + you + -ing? (the helping verb before the subject) · There are no + plural noun · wait for + person + to + base verb.
Notice (Activity 1): “Our father is very old. He cannot come with us.” Ask: “Does he want to come? Is he able to come? How do you know?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Build “Why aren’t you taking your sheep to drink water?” and ask “Where does aren’t go?”, then fix “There is no young men” and “wait for the other shepherds leave”.
Likely errors: *Why you aren’t taking … · *He cannot comes · *There is no young men · *wait the shepherds leave.
Use (Activity 4): a shared task at school or home (Why aren’t you …? … cannot … There are no … We wait for … to …).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Why-questions usually fall at the end: “WHY AREN’T you TAKing your SHEEP | to DRINK WAter?↘”
cannot: stress the first syllable, “he CANnot COME with us.”
Sheep /iː/ vs ship /ɪ/: make the long vowel clear.
-ed endings: helped /t/, happened /d/, understood (irregular).
Word focus: SIS-ters, EAR-ly (/ˈɜː.li/), SHEP-herds, un-der-STOOD, a-NOTH-er.
beforeReading: Show the well in the chapter picture. Ask: “Many people want water from one well. What problem can happen?” Collect ideas (a long queue, strong people go first).
duringReading: First listening: Why were the girls waiting?
Problem-solution chain in pairs, one quoted sentence per step.
Underline cannot and There are no.
Find the reason they came home early.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Look (Activity 1: cannot), Practise (Activity 2: build the Why question, Activity 3: there are no / wait for … to …), Use (Activity 4).
Write four sentences about a shared task and a helpful action.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: “Many people, one well: what problem can happen?”; 4–10 Listen with books closed (why were they waiting?), then listen and read along; 10–18 Problem-solution chain: Pairs put six sentence strips in order, then explain the chain to another pair using because; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (not willing or not able?), Activity 2 with a quick “question line” where learners ask each other Why aren’t you …-ing? about harmless class actions, Activity 3 in pairs; 30–38 Use: A shared task at school (the library queue, cleaning the board): pairs write four sentences with cannot, there are no, wait for … to … and so; 38–40 Exit ticket
discussionPoints: Why did the sisters wait far from the well?
What did Moses understand, and what did he do?
What makes help useful, not just kind words?
interactiveTips: Use the Waiting for Their Turn hotspot for the problem and the Water for the Sheep hotspot for Moses’s action.
Replay the sisters’ first answer before Activity 1.
Learners may read the sisters’ lines in pairs; nobody plays Moses.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chain with sentence strips to order and the frames “He cannot ____.” and “There are no ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a five-line dialogue about a shared task at school with one Why aren’t …-ing? question, cannot, there are no and wait for … to ….

formativeAssessment: Explains the problem with the sisters’ own words.
Puts aren’t before you in the question.
Uses there are no + plural and wait for + person + to + verb correctly.
expectedResponses: The sisters waited because their father was very old and could not come, and there were no young men in their house to help. Moses took their sheep to the water, so they came home early.
content.transferTask: Name one useful helping action for a real need at school or at home.
content.teacherReflection: Did the chain help learners see why cannot means “not able” here, and did they connect help with a real need?

classroomManagement.instructions: With your partner, put the six sentence strips in order. Then explain the chain to another pair with because.
checkQuestions: How many strips? (six)
What word do you use to explain? (because)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that the reason is in the sisters’ own words. In the question line, listen for “Why aren’t you …ing?” with aren’t before you. In the Use task, check there are no + plural.

rubric: there are no / wait for … to
exitTicket: Write one “Why aren’t you …-ing?” question and one sentence with “cannot”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains the problem with the sisters’ own words.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the sentence about their father.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses cannot for not able.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Not willing or not able?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Puts aren’t before you in the question.
rubricLevels.notYet: Write the question on the board as a model.

rubricLevels.criterion: there are no / wait for … to
rubricLevels.secure: Uses there are no and wait for … to.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give one model of each.

interculturalFocus.notice: Moses helps two sisters who wait far from the well because the shepherds are men and are strong.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: How do people in Türkiye show courtesy to women and older people in public (giving a seat, letting them go first)? How do people do this in an English-speaking country ('Ladies first', 'After you')?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Customs of courtesy change across cultures and times. Learners focus on helping people who need help, not on gender roles.

objectives: Tell the new-life sequence: invitation → meal → job offer → marriage → decision after ten years.
Explain why Moses accepted the job and why Shu’ayb (pbuh) could not help his daughters.
Discover couldn’t, needed + noun and because for a reason, want to / decided to + base verb, and the time words Later and After ten years.
See gratitude in Shu’ayb’s wish to thank Moses.
content.pedagogy: Draw a life line on the board and let pairs place the events with the time words from the text (Later, After ten years). Keep the needs clear: Shu’ayb (pbuh) was very old, so he couldn’t help his daughters; Moses needed a job and a house. The first Language Focus activity asks why Moses said yes, so learners find because in the reasons they have just discussed.
anticipatedMisconceptions: It was Shu’ayb (pbuh) who could not help his daughters; Moses was the one who needed a job and a house.
Moses did not go back to Egypt at once: “After ten years, Moses decided to go back to Egypt.”
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: couldn’t + base verb (not able in the past) · needed + noun · because for the reason of a choice · want to / decided to + base verb · Later and After ten years to move time forward.
Notice (Activity 1): “Moses accepted the job because he was a stranger in Midian. He needed a job and a house.” Ask: “Why did Moses say yes? Which word gives the reason?” Pairs complete couldn’t / because / needed.
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose to thank / to go and ask “What comes after want and decided?”, then order four sentences and circle the time words.
Likely errors: *I want thank him · *decided go · *needed to a job · *After ten year.
Use (Activity 4): a new opportunity (joining a club or team): I want to … because … I needed … Later … After two months, I decided to ….
content.pronunciationFocus:
Chunk the reason: “MOses acCEPTed the JOB | because he was a STRANger in MIDian.”
want to: say /ˈwɒnt tə/ with a weak to: “I WANT to THANK him.”
-ed endings: offered /d/, accepted /ɪd/, needed /ɪd/, helped /t/, married /d/, decided /ɪd/.
Word focus: Şu-AYB (shu-AYB), STRAN-ger (/dʒ/), ac-CEPT-ed, MAR-ried, de-CID-ed, FAM-i-ly.
beforeReading: Recall the end of Chapter 8: what did the sisters tell their father? Ask: “What will the father do now?” Keep predictions on the board.
duringReading: First listening: What did the father want to do?
Life line in pairs: Place five events and the time words.
Mark who needed what: Shu’ayb (pbuh) / Moses.
Underline want to and decided to.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Look (Activity 1: couldn’t, needed, because), Practise (Activity 2: want to / decided to, Activity 3: order the new life), Use (Activity 4).
Write four or five sentences about a new opportunity.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: “What will the father do now?” predictions; 4–10 Listen with books closed (what did the father want?), then listen and read along; 10–18 Life line on the board: Pairs place five events with Later and After ten years, then a “who needed what?” check (Shu’ayb (pbuh) / Moses); 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Why did Moses say yes?), Activities 2–3 in pairs; 30–38 Use: Chain story in groups of four about joining a new club, each learner adds one sentence (I want to … / I needed … / Later … / After two months, I decided to …), then each group writes its chain; 38–40 Exit ticket
discussionPoints: Why did Shu’ayb (pbuh) invite Moses?
Why did Moses accept the job?
How can we show thanks to someone who helped us?
interactiveTips: Use the Prophet Shu’ayb hotspot for the invitation and the A Home in Midian hotspot for the life line.
Replay the because sentence before Activity 1.
Nobody acts Shu’ayb (pbuh) or Moses; learners retell in the third person.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the life line with the events written and the time words missing, and the frames “He couldn’t ____.”, “He needed ____.” and “He decided to ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write six sentences about a new opportunity using needed, because, want to, Later, After … and decided to.

formativeAssessment: Keeps the two needs apart (Shu’ayb (pbuh) / Moses).
Uses to + base verb after want and decided.
Orders events with Later and After ten years.
expectedResponses: Shu’ayb (pbuh) was very old, so he couldn’t help his daughters. He wanted to thank Moses and offered him a job. Moses accepted because he was a stranger in Midian and needed a job and a house. Later he married one of the sisters, and after ten years he decided to go back to Egypt.
content.transferTask: Describe one way to show thanks through action.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners keep who needed what clear, and did the life line help them use Later and After ten years?

classroomManagement.instructions: With your partner, put five events on the life line on the board. Use Later and After ten years. Then check who needed what.
checkQuestions: Which two time words do you use? (Later, After ten years)
What do we check? (who needed what)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that Shu’ayb’s need and Moses’s need are kept apart. In groups of four, listen for want to and decided to. Make sure each group writes its chain.

exitTicket: Complete: “I want to ____ because ____. Later, I decided to ____.”

rubricLevels.secure: Puts the events on the life line in order.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the five events on cards.

rubricLevels.secure: Keeps the two needs apart.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “What did Shu’ayb need? What did Moses need?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses to + base verb after want and decided.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “He decided to …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Orders events with Later and After ten years.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the time words in the text.

interculturalFocus.notice: Shu'ayb invites Moses for a meal and offers him a job. Hospitality to a stranger is shared by many cultures.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: What does a Turkish family do when a guest comes (çay, food, 'Hoş geldiniz')? What do English speakers say ('Welcome', 'Come in', 'Make yourself at home')?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners practise welcoming phrases in both languages and avoid saying one culture is more welcoming.

content.chapter: Chapter 10 — The Voice on the Mountain
objectives: Build the setting: Winter, nobody on the way, getting dark and cold, a valley between mountains.
Follow the sequence: The fire → Moses climbs → the call → the instruction → the walking stick turns into a snake.
Discover when the chapter uses It was and when There was, how It was getting + adjective shows a slow change, and how Moses’s words give an instruction, a plan and a purpose; use turned into.
Read the sacred words respectfully and exactly as written.
content.pedagogy: Read slowly. First build the setting with two columns on the board: “It was …” (winter, getting dark and cold) and “There was …” (nobody on the way). This board is the first Language Focus task, so learners discover the difference themselves. The words the story gives as Allah’s are read once, calmly, by the teacher or the audio; they are not practised, acted or illustrated.
priorKnowledge: It is cold / There is a …, will for a plan, to + verb for purpose.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The hotspots show the fire and the walking stick; nothing shows the voice, and learners should not imagine or draw it.
“It was getting dark” (slowly changing) is different from “It was already dark” (the change has finished).
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: It was + season / weather / time vs There was + nobody / something · It was getting + adjective for a slow change · Wait here (instruction) + I will + base verb (plan) + to + base verb (purpose) · turned into + noun · Suddenly.
Notice (Activity 1): “It was winter. There was nobody on the way. It was getting dark and cold.” Ask: “Which sentence tells us the season or the weather? Which tells us if someone is on the road?”
Build (Activities 2–3): build “Wait here. I will get some fire to get warm.” and ask “Where does the reason go?”, then match valley, Suddenly, silence, chose and turned into.
Likely errors: *There was winter · *It was nobody · *It was get dark · *I will get some fire for get warm · *turned to a snake.
Use (Activity 4): a cold evening on a school trip (It was getting … . There was … . Wait here. I will … to …).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Slow change: “it was GETting DARK | and COLD.”
Three short parts with a pause: “WAIT here. | I will GET some FIRE | to get WARM.”
The sacred words are read calmly by the teacher or the audio, without drama.
-ed endings: started /ɪd/, traveled /d/, climbed /d/ (the b is silent), turned /d/.
Word focus: HILL-side, SI-lence (/ˈsaɪ.ləns/), SUD-den-ly, VAL-ley, WALK-ing stick (the l is silent).
beforeReading: Recall: Moses decided to go back to Egypt with his family. Ask: “What can be difficult on a long journey in winter?” Collect ideas (cold, dark, nobody to help).
duringReading: First listening: What did Moses see on the hillside?
Two columns: It was … / There was …, copied from the text.
Number the events from the fire to the snake.
Underline getting dark and already dark.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Look (Activity 1: It or There?), Practise (Activity 2: Moses’s plan, Activity 3: words from the mountain), Use (Activity 4).
Write four sentences about a cold evening on a school trip.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: “What is difficult on a long journey in winter?” ideas on the board; 4–11 Listen with books closed (what did Moses see?), then listen and read along, the sacred words read once calmly by the audio or the teacher; 11–18 Setting board in pairs: It was … / There was … columns, then number six events from the fire to the snake; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 checks the setting board, Activity 2 as whole-class building (where does the reason go?), Activity 3 in pairs; 30–38 Use: Pairs describe a cold evening on a school trip (It was getting … . There was nobody … . Wait here. I will … to …), then read it to another pair; 38–40 Exit ticket
discussionPoints: What was the weather like, and why did Moses go toward the fire?
What did Moses say to his family, and why?
What happened to the walking stick?
interactiveTips: Use the Fire on the Hillside hotspot for the setting and The Walking Stick hotspot for the last sentence.
Replay “It was getting dark and cold” and “It was already dark” one after the other.
Do not add images or descriptions of the voice.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the setting board with the first words and the frames “It was getting ____.”, “There was ____.” and “I will ____ to ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write five sentences about a changing evening using It was, There was, getting + adjective, one instruction and I will … to ….

formativeAssessment: Builds the setting and the order of events from the text.
Chooses It was / There was correctly.
Uses I will + verb and to + verb for plan and purpose.
expectedResponses: It was winter and it was getting dark and cold. Moses saw a fire and said to his family, “Wait here. I will get some fire to get warm.” On the mountain he heard a voice, and when he put down his walking stick, it turned into a big snake.
content.transferTask: Describe a safe plan for a cold evening with one instruction and one purpose sentence (to + verb).
content.teacherReflection: Did the setting board lead learners to the It / There rule, and were the sacred words read respectfully without invented detail?

classroomManagement.instructions: With your partner, fill the setting board: It was … and There was …. Then number six events from the fire to the snake.
checkQuestions: What are the two columns? (It was, There was)
How many events do you number? (six)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Make sure the sacred words are read once calmly, by the audio or by you. Check the setting columns. In the Use task, listen for “I will … to …”.

exitTicket: Write one “It was getting …” sentence and one “I will … to …” sentence about today.

rubricLevels.secure: Builds the setting and the order of events from the text.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the six events on cards.

rubricLevels.secure: Chooses It was or There was correctly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Is it the weather, or a thing?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses I will + verb and to + verb for plan and purpose.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “Wait here. I will … to …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Reads the sacred words with respect and without change.
rubricLevels.notYet: Model the calm reading.

interculturalFocus.notice: Moses sees a fire on a cold winter night in a valley between mountains.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: What do people do on cold winter evenings in Türkiye (soba, tea, family visits)? What do people do in a cold country such as Canada or Scotland (a fireplace, hot chocolate)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners describe winter customs they know. Families keep warm in many ways; none is better.

objectives: Identify the second sign (the shining hand), Moses’s mission and Harun’s support.
Tell instructions from story events in the chapter.
Discover that instructions start with the base verb and have no subject, that became and made him show a new role, and use did not + base verb, took … with him and to + verb for purpose.
See how a companion supports a difficult task.
content.pedagogy: Build a mission card on the board: What was Moses told to do? / What did he become? / Who went with him? / Why did he go to the palace? Learners fill it with quoted phrases. Then the first Language Focus activity sorts instructions and story events, so learners discover from the first word of each line whether it is an instruction. Allah’s words are read as they are and not rewritten.
priorKnowledge: Imperatives, became, to + verb for purpose.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The chapter is not only about the shining hand: It also gives Moses a mission to go to the king.
The king and his helpers did not believe in Allah.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: instruction (base verb, no subject: Put …, take …, Go …) vs story event (subject + past verb: Moses went, He met) · became + noun and made + person + noun for a new role · did not + base verb · took + person + with him · to + base verb for purpose.
Notice (Activity 1): pairs sort six parts of the chapter. Ask: “Look at the first word. Is someone told what to do, or does the story tell us what happened?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose became / did not / made, then complete with / to and ask “Who went with Moses? Why did he go?”
Likely errors: *Moses become a prophet · *they did not believed · *made him to His prophet · *went to the palace for give the message.
Use (Activity 4): a small mission at school (Go to the library. Take a friend with you. We went there to return the books.).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Instructions fall at the end: “PUT your HAND into your CHEST. | NOW TAKE it OUT.”
Chunk companion and purpose: “MOses took his BROther haRUN with him | and WENT to the PALace | to GIVE the MESsage of alLAH.”
Word focus: SHIN-ing, PROPH-et (sounds like profit), ha-RUN, THRONE (/θ/, not /t/), MES-sage, POW-er-ful.
beforeReading: Recall the first sign in Chapter 10 (the walking stick). Ask: “Chapter 11 is called The Signs of Allah. What might come next?”
duringReading: First listening: What happened to Moses’s hand?
Mission card in pairs, one quoted phrase per line.
Mark I (instruction) or E (story event) next to six sentences.
Underline became and made.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Look (Activity 1: instruction or story event?), Practise (Activity 2: a new role, Activity 3: with whom? why?), Use (Activity 4).
Write a small school mission in four sentences.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: Recall the first sign, predict the next one; 4–10 Listen with books closed (what happened to his hand?), then listen and read along; 10–18 Mission card in pairs (told to do / became / went with / why), then mark six sentences I or E; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 checks the I / E marks, Activities 2–3 in pairs with the questions “Who? Why?”; 30–38 Use: Mission cards for school, pairs write a small mission (Go to … . Take … with you. We went there to …) and swap cards with another pair, who explain it back; 38–40 Exit ticket
discussionPoints: What was the second sign?
What was Moses told to do?
How did Harun support Moses?
interactiveTips: Use The Shining Hand hotspot for the sign and the Harun hotspot for the mission card.
Replay the last sentence of the chapter so learners see the palace scene.
Read Allah’s words exactly as written.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the mission card with the questions and the frames “He became ____.”, “He took ____ with him.” and “He went to ____ to ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write five sentences about a mission using one instruction, became, took … with …, to + verb and did not.

formativeAssessment: Names the sign, the mission and the helper.
Tells an instruction from a story event by the first word.
Uses became, took … with him and to + verb accurately.
expectedResponses: Moses put his hand into his chest and took it out, and it was shining. Allah told him to go to the king. Moses became a prophet. He took his brother Harun with him and went to the palace to give the message of Allah.
content.transferTask: Describe how a friend can support you in a difficult but safe task.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners use the first word to tell instructions from events, and did the mission and the helper stay as important as the sign?

classroomManagement.instructions: With your partner, fill the mission card: told to do, became, went with, why. Then mark six sentences I for instruction or E for event.
checkQuestions: How many parts on the card? (four)
What does I mean? (an instruction)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check the I and E marks by the first word of each sentence. Listen for “Who? Why?” in Activities 2–3. In the card swap, check that the other pair can explain the mission back.

exitTicket: Write one instruction for a friend and one sentence with “took … with me … to …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Names the sign, the mission and the helper.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask three questions: what sign, what job, who helped.

rubricLevels.secure: Tells an instruction from an event by the first word.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Does it start with a verb?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses became and made correctly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give one gap sentence for each.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses with and to + verb correctly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “He took … with him to …”.

interculturalFocus.notice: Moses is given a mission, and his brother Harun (Aaron in English) supports him.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: How do brothers and sisters help each other in Turkish families (abi, abla)? Are there special words for an older brother or sister in English (there are not; English uses 'big brother', 'older sister')?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners notice that Turkish has respectful words for older siblings that English does not. Language reflects family culture.

objectives: Identify Moses’s message and the two signs he showed.
Separate what the story says (These were miracles of Allah) from the king’s opinion and claim (crazy, only magic).
Discover that thought + sentence gives an opinion, and use told + person + about, decided to + base verb, can + base verb (no to) and Then.
Check evidence before repeating someone’s claim.
content.pedagogy: Two voices organize the lesson: Pairs sort sentences into “The story says …” and “The king says / thinks …”. This makes the first meaning question easy: “He thought Moses was crazy — a fact or the king’s opinion?” Learners then order the two signs with Then and see that the story calls them miracles, while the king calls them magic.
priorKnowledge: said / told, direct speech, can for ability.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “This is only magic” is the king’s claim; the story says “These were miracles of Allah.”
“He thought Moses was crazy” is the king’s opinion, not a fact in the story.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: meaning of universe, crazy, miracles, made fun of · thought + sentence for an opinion · told + person + about · decided to + base verb · can + base verb (no to) · Then for the next step.
Notice (Activity 1): pairs match four words with their meanings. Then ask: “He thought Moses was crazy. Is this a fact in the story or the king’s opinion? How do you know?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose told / to show / do and ask “Which verb takes a person directly?”, then order the two signs and circle Then.
Likely errors: *Moses said him about Allah · *decided show · *can to do · *Then he puts (present in a past story).
Use (Activity 4): Show and explain a school experiment (I told my friend about … . He thought … . I decided to … . Then … . Our class can …).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Contrast the two voices with stress: “these were MIRacles of alLAH” / “this is ONly MAGic”.
Pause after Then: “THEN | he put his ARM in his ARMpit.”
-ed endings: listened /d/ (the t is silent), decided /ɪd/, laughed /t/ (/lɑːft/, gh = f).
Word focus: MIR-a-cles, U-ni-verse, MAG-ic (/dʒ/), ma-GI-cians, CRA-zy, ARM-pit.
beforeReading: Recall Moses’s mission from Chapter 11. Ask: “When Moses gives the message, how will the king react?” Keep predictions on the board.
duringReading: First listening: Did the king believe Moses?
Two voices in pairs: “The story says …” / “The king says or thinks …”.
Number the steps of the two signs.
Underline thought, decided to and can.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Look (Activity 1: words in the palace), Practise (Activity 2: told, decided to, can, Activity 3: the signs step by step), Use (Activity 4).
Write a short show-and-explain text about a school experiment.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: “How will the king react?” predictions; 4–10 Listen with books closed (did the king believe him?), then listen and read along; 10–18 Two-voices sort in pairs with sentence strips, then a whole-class check: Which words show the king’s opinion? (thought, only magic); 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 with the fact-or-opinion question, Activities 2–3 in pairs; 30–38 Use: Pairs describe a simple class experiment (I told … about … . He thought … . I decided to … . Then … . We can …), one pair presents; 38–40 Exit ticket
discussionPoints: What did Moses tell the king?
What does the story call the signs, and what does the king call them?
Why is it important to check evidence before we repeat what someone says?
interactiveTips: Use the Two Miracles hotspot for the story’s signs and The King Laughed hotspot for the king’s claim.
Replay the narrator’s sentence and the king’s sentence one after the other.
Keep the focus on the two voices, not on the snake detail.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the two-voice chart with the heads and three sentence strips, and the frames “He thought ____.”, “He decided to ____.” and “They can ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write five sentences about a claim and the evidence: Thought …, told … about …, decided to …, Then …, can ….

formativeAssessment: Keeps the story’s words and the king’s claim apart.
Explains thought + sentence as an opinion.
Uses told + person, decided to and can + base verb correctly.
expectedResponses: Moses told the king about Allah. The king thought Moses was crazy. Moses showed two signs: The stick turned into a big snake, and then his arm was shining white. The story says these were miracles of Allah, but the king said, “This is only magic.”
content.transferTask: Give one example of checking the evidence before repeating someone’s claim.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners keep the two voices apart throughout the lesson and the Use step?

classroomManagement.instructions: With your partner, sort the strips into two voices: what the story says and what the king says. Then find the words that show the king’s opinion.
checkQuestions: How many voices? (two)
What words show the king’s opinion? (thought, only magic)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that “These were miracles” goes to the story voice. In Activity 1, ask “fact or opinion?”. Choose one pair to present their class experiment.

exitTicket: Write one “I thought …” sentence and one “I decided to …” sentence about today.

rubricLevels.secure: Keeps the story’s words and the king’s claim apart.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Who says this?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains thought + sentence as an opinion.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Is it true, or what he thinks?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses told + person, decided to and can correctly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give one model of each.

rubricLevels.secure: Orders steps with Then.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “First … Then …”.

interculturalFocus.notice: The king calls Moses's signs 'only magic'. Every culture has words for tricks and for wonders.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: What is the difference between 'magic' (a trick) and 'a miracle' (a sign from Allah) in English? Which Turkish words match (sihir, büyü / mucize)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners keep the story's view and the king's view apart and explain the difference clearly.

objectives: Tell the turning point in order: The magicians arrive → sticks and ropes → Moses’s stick → the magicians believe.
Compare the magicians’ response with the king’s response.
