Discover the difference between a finished action (came, put down, bowed down) and an action in progress (were holding, were moving), and use threw, quickly, still did not, because and continued to.
Connect accepting clear evidence with humility.
content.pedagogy: A “Before / After” chart shows the turning point: The magicians before the sign and after it, and the king before and after. The magicians change, the king does not. The Language Focus then asks learners to treat the scene like a photo: “Which actions finished? Which were going on in the picture?” Learners discover the difference before you confirm it.
priorKnowledge: Past continuous from Chapters 5 and 7, because.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The magicians believed; the king still did not believe because he was arrogant.
The snake is not the main learning point: The change in the magicians and the king’s refusal are.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: past simple for a finished action (came, put down, bowed down) vs was/were + -ing for an action in progress (were holding, were moving) · threw (irregular) · quickly (how) · still + did not · because · continued to + base verb.
Notice (Activity 1): pairs sort five parts of the chapter. Ask: “Did the action finish, or was it going on, like a photo of the moment?”
Build (Activities 2–3): fix throwed / quick, then complete still / because / to and ask “Did the king change? Which word tells us?”
Likely errors: *throwed · *His stick quick ate · *The king did not still believe · *continued hurt.
Use (Activity 4): a small class demonstration (We came with … . Some were holding … . Put … . It turned into … . It happened quickly.).
content.pronunciationFocus:
threw /θruː/: tongue between the teeth, not /truː/ or /fruː/.
Stress on STILL: “the KING STILL did not beLIEVE in alLAH, | beCAUSE he was ARrogant.”
bowed /baʊd/ rhymes with loud.
-ed endings: invited /ɪd/, bowed /d/, shouted /ɪd/, continued /d/.
Word focus: AR-ro-gant, in-VIT-ed, HUGE (/hjuːdʒ/), con-TIN-ued, QUICK-ly.
beforeReading: Ask: “When you see clear evidence that your answer is wrong, what do you do?” Collect two honest answers.
duringReading: First listening: What did the magicians shout?
Before / After chart: The magicians and the king.
Mark F (finished) or P (in progress) next to five actions.
Underline still, because and continued to.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Look (Activity 1: finished or in progress?), Practise (Activity 2: threw and quickly, Activity 3: still, because, continued to), Use (Activity 4).
Write four sentences about a small class demonstration.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: “What do you do when evidence shows you are wrong?”; 4–10 Listen with books closed (what did the magicians shout?), then listen and read along; 10–18 Before / After chart in pairs for the magicians and the king, then a whole-class sentence: “The magicians believed, but the king still did not believe because …”; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 as a “photo or finished?” discovery, Activities 2–3 in pairs; 30–38 Use: Pairs describe a simple class demonstration (We came with … . Some were holding … . Put … . It turned into … . It happened quickly.), then read it to the class; 38–40 Exit ticket
discussionPoints: What did the magicians do after they saw Moses’s stick?
Why did the king still not believe?
What can we do when clear evidence changes what we think?
interactiveTips: Use The Huge Snake hotspot for the event and the Bowing Down hotspot for the response.
Replay the last three sentences before Activity 3.
Do not act the snakes or the magicians; use the chart.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the Before / After chart with first words and the frames “The magicians ____, but the king still ____ because ____.” and “He continued to ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write five sentences comparing two reactions to the same evidence using still, because and continued to, plus one was/were + -ing sentence.

formativeAssessment: Orders the turning point correctly.
Separates finished actions from actions in progress.
Uses still did not, because and continued to accurately.
expectedResponses: The magicians put down their sticks and ropes, and they were moving like snakes. Moses threw down his stick and it quickly ate all the snakes. The magicians believed in the Lord of Moses and Harun, but the king still did not believe because he was arrogant, and he continued to hurt Moses and his people.
content.transferTask: Give one school example of changing your answer after clear evidence.
content.teacherReflection: Did the chart show the turning point clearly, and did learners link humility with the magicians’ response, not with a slogan?

classroomManagement.instructions: With your partner, make a Before and After chart for the magicians and the king. Then finish this sentence together: “The magicians believed, but the king still did not believe because …”.
checkQuestions: How many people or groups in the chart? (two: the magicians and the king)
What sentence do we finish? (the still did not believe sentence)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that the king’s After box is the same as his Before box. In Activity 1, ask “photo or finished?”. In the Use task, listen for quickly.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “still did not” and one with “continued to” about a real situation.

rubricLevels.secure: Orders the turning point.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the steps on cards.

rubricLevels.secure: Separates finished actions from actions in progress.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Was it moving, or did it finish?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses threw and quickly correctly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the sentence in the text.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses still, because and continued to.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “He still did not … because …”.

interculturalFocus.notice: The magicians see the truth and believe, even though the king threatens them.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which English phrases describe changing your mind because of evidence ('I stand corrected', 'You're right, I was wrong')? Which Turkish phrases do the same ('Haklısın, yanılmışım')?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Changing your mind is respected in many cultures. Learners practise one phrase in each language.

objectives: Explain why life became harder and why the people left at night.
Explain why the caravan moved slowly and where they arrived at sunrise.
Discover that “We are going away” tells a plan that has not happened yet, and use Get ready for, must + base verb, could not + base verb, slowly and When + past.
Plan for everyone in a group, including slower members.
content.pedagogy: Treat the chapter as a journey plan. Pairs complete a planning card from Moses’s words (Get ready / We must / We will leave) and then a timeline (night → sunrise → the sea). The first Language Focus activity asks: “When Moses said this, were they already far away?” Learners discover from the timeline that “We are going away” is a plan.
priorKnowledge: will for plans, could not, adverbs such as quickly.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “We are going away from Egypt” is a plan; the people had not left yet.
The caravan moved slowly because the children and the old could not walk fast, not because the people did not want to go.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: Get ready for (instruction) and We are going away (a plan for the near future) · must + base verb (necessary) · could not + base verb (past inability) · slowly (how the caravan moved) · When + past for time.
Notice (Activity 1): Read Moses’s words and decide true or false: “When Moses said this, the people were already far away from Egypt.” Ask: “Had they left yet? Which words tell us it is a plan?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Match keep it secret, Life became harder, caravan, got tired and rose, and ask “What does must tell us?”, then choose could not / slowly / When.
Likely errors: *must to keep · *could not walked · *moved slow · *When the sun rises (present in a past story).
Use (Activity 4): Plan a quiet class trip (Get ready for … . We are going … . We must … . We will leave at … . The small children could not …, so we walked slowly.).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Plan and duty: “we are GOing aWAY from EGypt”, “you MUST keep it SEcret”.
-ly endings are clear but short: SLOW-ly, QUICK-ly.
-ed endings: asked /t/, called /d/, moved /d/, prepared /d/, arrived /d/.
Word focus: JOUR-ney (/ˈdʒɜː.ni/), SE-cret, CAR-a-van, AR-my, pre-PARED.
beforeReading: Recall: After Chapter 13 the king continued to hurt Moses and his people. Ask: “What can a large group with children and old people do in danger?”
duringReading: First listening: When did they leave Egypt?
Planning card from Moses’s words: instruction / must / will.
Timeline: night → sunrise → the sea.
Underline could not and slowly.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Look (Activity 1: a plan for the journey), Practise (Activity 2: night journey words, Activity 3: could not, slowly, When), Use (Activity 4).
Write a plan for a quiet class trip in five sentences.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: “What can a big group with children and old people do in danger?”; 4–10 Listen with books closed (when did they leave?), then listen and read along; 10–18 Planning card and timeline in pairs, then a whole-class check of why the caravan moved slowly; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (had they left yet?), Activities 2–3 in pairs; 30–38 Use: Groups of three plan a quiet class trip that includes younger or slower members (Get ready for … . We are going … . We must … . We will leave at … . The small children could not …, so we walked slowly.), each group reads its plan; 38–40 Exit ticket
discussionPoints: Why did life become harder for Moses’s people?
Why must they keep the journey secret?
Why did the caravan move slowly, and how can we plan for slower members of a group?
interactiveTips: Use the Leaving at Night hotspot for the planning card and The Caravan hotspot for the timeline.
Replay the sentence about the children and the old before Activity 3.
Keep travel details to the text.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the planning card with the verbs written and the frames “We must ____.”, “We will ____.” and “They could not ____, so ____ slowly.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write six sentences for a trip plan using Get ready for, are going, must, will, could not, slowly and When.

formativeAssessment: Explains why they left at night and moved slowly.
Understands “We are going away” as a plan.
Uses must + base verb, could not + base verb and slowly correctly.
expectedResponses: Moses told his people, “Get ready for the journey … you must keep it secret.” They left Egypt at night. The children and the old could not walk fast, so the caravan moved slowly. When the sun rose, they arrived at the sea.
content.transferTask: Plan a small safe trip with one instruction, one must sentence and one will sentence, and include a slower group member.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners discover that “are going” can be a plan, and did the Use step include the needs of slower members?

classroomManagement.instructions: With your partner, fill the planning card and the timeline. Then check with the class why the caravan moved slowly.
checkQuestions: What do you fill? (the planning card and the timeline)

objectives: Describe the problem: The sea in front of them and the army behind them.
Order the rescue: Moses hits the sea → the sea parts → walls of water → sandy ground → they walk safely.
Discover the position words in front of and behind, and use became, could see, safely, will + base verb and caught.
Notice how Moses calmed his people.
content.pedagogy: Start with a desk-top diagram: Each pair uses a pencil case for the sea, a ruler for the army and an eraser for the people, and places them as the text says. The first Language Focus activity checks the diagram, so position words are discovered from a model, not from a list. Nobody acts the crossing; the words the story gives as Allah’s are read as they are.
priorKnowledge: Prepositions of place (in, on, near), will, past simple.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The sea was in front of them and the army was behind them: “They had no place to escape.”
Moses calmed his people before the sea opened: “Calm down! Allah is with us and will help us go to a safe place.”
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: in front of / behind for position and with (Allah was with them) · became + noun (the waves became high walls) · could see (now possible) · safely walked between · will + base verb (no -s) · caught (irregular) in catch up with.
Notice (Activity 1): pairs complete in front of / behind / with and check the desk-top diagram. Ask: “Where was the sea? Where was the army? Why could they not escape?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Order the rescue and ask “What was possible now?” (could see), then fix “will helps” and “catched”.
Likely errors: *in front them · *will helps · *catched · *walked safe.
Use (Activity 4): a safe route through a crowded corridor at break time (The canteen is in front of us. The stairs are behind us. Calm down! We will …).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Calm reassurance with a steady voice: “CALM DOWN! | alLAH is WITH us | and will HELP us | go to a SAFE PLACE.”
Position chunks: “in FRONT of them”, “beHIND them”, “beTWEEN the WALLS”.
-ed endings: panicked /t/, parted /ɪd/, walked /t/, caught /kɔːt/ (gh silent).
Word focus: PAN-icked, PART-ed, SAFE-ly, es-CAPE, SAN-dy.
beforeReading: Recall the end of Chapter 14: they arrived at the sea and the king prepared his huge army. Ask: “What is the problem now?”
duringReading: First listening: How did the people feel?
Desk-top diagram: sea / army / people, placed as the text says.
Underline Moses’s words to his people.
Number the steps of the rescue.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Look (Activity 1: in front of, behind, with), Practise (Activity 2: the sea opens, Activity 3: will help and caught), Use (Activity 4).
Write a safe route through a crowded place with position words.

Calm down! We will … . We walked safely between …), then guide another pair through it; 38–40 Exit ticket

What did Moses say to calm them?
What changed after Moses hit the sea?

content.chapter: Chapter 16 — The Cruel King Died in the Water
objectives: Retell the final events calmly and in order.
Separate the king’s claim (“I told the sea to open”) from what the story says happened, and find the two lessons the story states.

Discover that “It tells us that …” and “It shows that …” introduce a lesson in the present simple, and use said to + person, told + person/thing + to + base verb and the place and time words very close behind, midway and In the end.
Connect the lesson “no one can own another person” with respect for every person.
content.pedagogy: The final chapter closes the story. Learners first order the final events and mark the king’s words as a claim (Chapter 15 said that Allah made a road in the sea). Then they find the two lessons and notice that the verbs change: “Why does the story say tells and shows, not told and showed?” Learners discover that a lesson is always true. The drowning is read once and not discussed in detail.
priorKnowledge: said / told from Chapter 12, when + past, present simple.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “I told the sea to open, and it opened” is the king’s claim; Chapter 15 says that Allah made a road in the sea.
The two lessons are the story’s own: No one can own another person, and only Allah has power over us.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: It tells us that … / It shows that … + present simple for a lesson · said to + person · told + person/thing + to + base verb · place and time words (very close behind, entered, midway, In the end, no one).
Notice (Activity 1): “It tells us that no one can own another person. It shows that only Allah has power over us.” Ask: “Is this a new event, the king’s words or a lesson? Why tells and shows, not told and showed?”
Build (Activities 2–3): fix “said his soldiers” and “told the sea open”, then match very close behind, entered, midway, In the end and no one with their meanings.
Likely errors: *The king said his soldiers · *told the sea open · *told to the sea · *It told us that (past for a lesson) · *No one can owns.
Use (Activity 4): a short everyday story and its lesson (In the end, … . It tells us that … . It shows that …).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Lesson sentences with steady stress: “it TELLS us | that NO ONE can OWN a-NOTH-er PERson.” / “it SHOWS | that ONly alLAH | has POWer over us.”
Pause after the reporting verb: “the KING SAID to his SOLdiers, | ‘LOOK! …’”
-ed endings: opened /d/, entered /d/, closed /d/, died /d/.
Word focus: mid-WAY, LES-sons, POW-er, SOL-diers, EN-tered. Read the drowning sentence calmly.
beforeReading: Recall Chapter 15 with the desk-top diagram from memory: Where are Moses’s people now? Where is the king?
duringReading: First listening: What did the king say to his soldiers?
Order four final events with When and In the end.
Mark the king’s words as “claim”.
Box the two lesson sentences.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Look (Activity 1: what do these sentences give us?), Practise (Activity 2: said to, told … to, Activity 3: place and time words), Use (Activity 4).
Write a short everyday story with a lesson.
Continue with Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge and Language Review before the Final Challenge.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: Retell Chapter 15 from memory in three pair sentences; 4–10 Listen with books closed (what did the king say?), then listen and read along calmly; 10–17 Claim or story? Pairs sort four sentences (the king’s words / what happened / the lessons), then box the two lessons; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–29 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Why tells, not told?), Activities 2–3 in pairs; 29–35 Whole-story line: Groups put six cards from Chapters 1–16 in order and read them aloud; 35–38 Use: Learners write a two-sentence everyday story and one lesson (In the end, … . It shows that …); 38–40 Exit ticket
discussionPoints: What did the king claim, and what does Chapter 15 say happened?
What are the two lessons the story tells us?
What can we do at school to show that no one can own another person? (your own idea)
interactiveTips: Use The Closed Sea hotspot only for the order of events and the Only Allah hotspot for the two lesson sentences.
Replay the king’s words and the lesson sentences separately.
Follow the review order: Knowledge Check → Vocabulary Challenge → Language Review → Master Glossary → Final Challenge.

differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a six-event summary of the whole book and finish with one lesson sentence (It shows that …) and one of your own ideas, labelled as yours.

Uses said to, told … to and It tells us that … accurately.
expectedResponses: The king said to his soldiers, “Look! I told the sea to open, and it opened.” They entered the waters, and when they were midway, Allah closed the sea over them. The story tells us that no one can own another person, and it shows that only Allah has power over us.
content.transferTask: Give one everyday action that respects another person’s freedom and dignity, and label it as your own idea.
content.teacherReflection: Did the ending stay calm and source-faithful, and did learners discover why lessons use the present simple?

classroomManagement.instructions: With your partner, sort four sentences: the king’s words, what happened, the lessons. Box the two lessons. Later, put six cards from the whole book in order.
checkQuestions: How many lessons do you box? (two)
How many cards for the whole book? (six)

metadata.title: Teacher Guide — Prophet Moses (A2)
metadata.subtitle: TYMM-aligned A2 guide with chapter-specific support, grammar discovered from the story and 40-minute lesson plans
metadata.estimatedDuration: 16 chapter lessons of 40 minutes each. The whole-book review pages (Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review, Master Glossary, Final Challenge) follow separately.
metadata.targetAudience: Lower-secondary learners studying English at approximately CEFR A2.
metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow a short, supported story, find a sentence that proves an answer and say or write three or four short connected sentences with a frame.
metadata.purpose: Develop A2 listening, reading, speaking and writing through the story of Prophet Moses (pbuh), using the chapter’s own sentences for evidence, the Language Focus attached to every chapter and short transfer about the learners’ own world.
metadata.approachDesc: Every chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading come first: Learners understand the story and prove answers with a sentence from the text, and the Quick Challenge checks the key idea. Grammar is then learned inductively, as the Maarif Model expects for English: In the Language Focus learners first LOOK at a real sentence from the chapter and answer a meaning question (One person or a group? Did it happen or is it a plan?), say the rule in their own words, and only then does the teacher confirm it. Next they PRACTISE the form in the chapter’s own sentences, and finally USE it in three or four short sentences about their own life (YDAB3 speaking, YDAB4 writing). At A2 steps are short and concrete, frames are strong and every piece of writing is rehearsed orally first. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/yabanci-dil-alan-becerileri.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 16 Quick Challenges, evidence sentences, Language Focus answers (Look → Practise → Use), short spoken and written transfer, exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and Final Challenge.

readingFramework.before: A short, chapter-specific hook (picture, title, event cards, a question or a drawing on the board) that activates only what this chapter needs. Predictions stay predictions until the text confirms them.
readingFramework.during: Listen first with books closed for one gist question, then listen and read along. Learners then return to the text for one clear job: Who’s who, order of events, reason and result, what people were doing, who is speaking, or where things are.
readingFramework.after: Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (Look → Practise → Use), then three or four short sentences about the learners’ own world and a one-line exit ticket.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Start with the chapter’s Word Notes and add only the words learners need for the task (for example shepherds, well, caravan).
vocabularyApproach.method: Guess from the sentence, the picture or a hotspot first, then check the Word Note. Say the word with its stress before writing it.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse the words in the Use step, the exit ticket and the whole-book review pages.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based. Start from the story sentence, ask one meaning question (Who? One or more? Finished or still going on? A plan or a fact?), let pairs say the rule in their own words and only then confirm it with the explanation in the app. Practise the form in the chapter’s own sentences and use it in a new, safe situation. Do not replace the chapter work with unrelated grammar drills.
grammarSequence: Ch1: was / were · believed in · did not + base verb · Because of + noun
Ch2: irregular past verbs · past (burnt) vs will + verb for a prediction · One day / Then / When + past
Ch3: could (possible danger) vs could not (not able) · imperatives + will for a promise · told + person + to · kinder than
Ch4: movement + to vs near / nearby · different from · I will (decision) · imperative (order)
Ch5: take care of / look after · grew up / became · always · because + clause · was walking … saw
Ch6: accidentally · to + verb (purpose) · because · are looking (now) vs are going to catch (expected)
Ch7: there were · were + -ing for a scene · arrived at · So · look for
Ch8: cannot · Why aren’t you + -ing? · there are no + plural · wait for + person + to
Ch9: couldn’t · needed + noun · because · want to / decided to · Later / After ten years
Ch10: It was vs There was · was getting + adjective · Wait here + I will … to … · turned into
Ch11: instruction vs story event · became / made him · did not · took … with him · to + verb
Ch12: thought + sentence (opinion) · told + person + about · decided to · can + verb · Then
Ch13: finished action vs was/were + -ing · threw · quickly · still did not · because · continued to
Ch14: Get ready for / We are going (plan) · must · could not · slowly · When + past
Ch15: in front of / behind / with · became · could see · safely · will help · caught
Ch16: It tells us that / It shows that · said to · told + person/thing + to · place and time words

skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: find the sentence that proves an answer, follow the order of events, see a simple reason and result, and tell a character’s words or opinion from what the story says happened.
skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: listen for gist with books closed, then listen again for one detail, a time word or a target sentence.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: retell in short steps, ask and answer Why? questions, give a safe instruction, a promise or a warning, and rehearse the Use sentences orally.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: write three or four short connected sentences with a frame, using the chapter’s pattern in a new situation, then check one form with a partner.

valuesFocus: D1 Justice — notice unfair use of power and name a fair alternative
D9 Compassion — notice someone who suffers or needs care
D12 Patience — stay calm in fear and difficulty
D16 Responsibility — admit a mistake and take the next right step
D20 Helpfulness — see a real need and help in a useful way
D6 Honesty — separate what a character claims from what the story shows
D10 Humility — accept clear evidence even when it changes our view
D11 Freedom — no one can own another person
D14 Respect — protect human dignity and handle sacred scenes respectfully
languageFocus: Every one of the 16 story chapters has a Language Focus set built as Look → Practise → Use.
Use it after listening, reading and the Quick Challenge, never before the story is understood.
Always start from the story sentence and ask a meaning question before naming the form.
Let learners answer first; the explanation shown after each answer confirms the rule they have found.
The last step is always three or four short sentences about the learners’ own world, rehearsed orally before writing, not a retelling of the chapter.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Lower the language load, not the thinking goal: One evidence sentence at a time, audio replay, picture cues, sentence frames with the first words written, oral rehearsal before writing and copying the target form from the text first. Extend by adding one more pattern or one more reason, never by adding facts that are not in the book.

sensitiveNotes.title: Content safeguards
notes: Qur’anic verses, words the story gives as Allah’s words, prophetic sayings and prayers (for example Moses’s dua in Chapter 6) and poem lines are read, explained and matched to meanings; they are never gapped by the teacher, corrected or rewritten. Where an app activity asks learners to complete such words (Chapter 3, Activity 2), let learners read the complete sentence from the story aloud afterwards.

Prophets are never acted, drawn or role-played by learners. Freeze-frames, role-plays and drawings use objects, places and non-prophet characters only; reading the story text aloud as it is written is fine.
Chapter 2 includes the killing of baby boys: Read it once, calmly, and focus on injustice, cause and consequence without detail or acting.
Chapter 6 includes an accidental death: Keep the text’s word “accidentally”, and focus on regret, forgiveness and the next safe action.
Chapters 10, 11 and 15 contain words the story gives as Allah’s: read them calmly, without images of the voice and without speculation beyond the text.

Chapter 12: keep the story’s words (“These were miracles of Allah”) separate from Pharaoh’s claim (“This is only magic”). Chapter 16: “I told the sea to open” is Pharaoh’s claim, not what the story says happened.
Chapter 16 includes drowning: Focus on the order of events and the two lessons the story states, not on detail.
Do not add legends, dates or details that are not in this A2 book.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: The story of Prophet Moses (pbuh) raises questions every community faces today: How power should be used, how we treat people who are new or weak, how we share what everyone needs, and why no person may own another.

themes.title: Power and fairness:
themes.description: Pharaoh forced the Children of Israel to do dangerous work for no money because of his fear (Chapter 1). Discuss fair rules for work and why leaders must not treat a group unfairly.

themes.title: Sharing what everyone needs:
themes.description: At the well the two sisters waited for their turn, and Moses helped them water their sheep (Chapters 7–8). Connect this with sharing water, queues and public places fairly today.

themes.title: Welcoming a stranger:
themes.description: Moses was a stranger in Midian and needed a job and a house; Shu’ayb (pbuh) offered him a job and a new life began (Chapter 9). Talk about how a school or town can welcome newcomers.

themes.title: Human dignity and freedom:
themes.description: The story tells us that no one can own another person (Chapter 16). Connect this with respect for every person’s rights, at school and in the world.

actions: Write three short class rules for sharing something everyone needs (the water fountain, the library, the ball at break time).
Make a “Welcome” card in simple English for a new student, with two things you can do to help them.
Finish the sentence “No one can own another person, so at school we …” with two fair actions.

exitTicket: One thing that happened in today’s chapter, and the sentence that proves it: …
One English pattern I noticed today, with my own example: …
One helpful or fair action I can do this week: …

miniProject.title: Helpers in the Story
miniProject.desc: In groups, choose three people who helped in Chapters 3–9 (for example Moses’s sister, Queen Asiye, Moses at the well, Shu’ayb (pbuh)). For each one, copy one sentence from the book that shows the help, then write two sentences about a helper in your own school or family. Use at least two Language Focus patterns, such as “told … to …”, “because …” or “wait for … to …”. Present your poster in two minutes. Do not draw the prophets.

reflectivePrompt.title: A Stranger in a New Place
reflectivePrompt.desc: Moses was a stranger in Midian. He needed a job and a house, and Shu’ayb (pbuh) offered him a job. Write four to six sentences about a time when you were new somewhere, or when someone was new in your class. What did they need? Who helped, and how?

valuesEducation.title: TYMM Values in Action
valuesEducation.description: Name a value only after learners point to a story action that shows it. Then ask for one small, observable action at school or at home. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.

items.label: D1 Justice
items.value: What fair action could replace Pharaoh’s unfair use of power?

items.label: D9 Compassion / D20 Helpfulness
items.value: Connect care with useful action: Asiye takes care of a baby, the sister finds a nurse, Moses waters the sisters’ sheep.

items.label: D16 Responsibility
items.value: After a mistake: feel sorry, ask for forgiveness, take the next safe step (Chapter 6).

items.label: D6 Honesty / D10 Humility
items.value: Separate a claim from evidence, and accept clear evidence like the magicians in Chapter 13.

items.label: D11 Freedom / D14 Respect
items.value: Connect the ending with human dignity: no one can own another person.

questions: Which story action shows this value?
What small action could show the same value at school or at home?
Which part is from the story and which part is your own idea?

test.title: End-of-Level Test A2
test.when: Give the test when the class has finished the A2 books it reads this term. It has four parts and takes about 60 minutes plus a short speaking test for each learner.
parts: Reading and Language (40 minutes): in the app. The learner gets a test code at the end.
Writing (20 minutes): on paper. Write an email to a friend about a visit to an old place. (50–70 words)
Speaking (about 6 minutes): one learner with the teacher, in 2 parts.
Scoring: type the test code in “Score a test”, then score Writing and Speaking with the bands. Copy the pilot line for the pilot results sheet.

professionalDevelopment.intro: Use these steps to plan your own development with this book: rate yourself on the EPG areas with this book’s chapters, let a colleague observe one of two lessons, keep a short log after each chapter, run one small classroom enquiry, work with colleagues, and agree on scoring before the End-of-Level Test.

peerObservation.focus: Explain how Moses came back to his mother and grew up in a safe place.
lookFor: Instruction: Each group writes one time card with a sentence from the story. Stand in order at the front. The class checks the order.
Check questions: How many cards does each group write? (one) / Who checks the order? (the class)
While learners work: Check the order of the time cards. In Activity 2, ask why because and not because of. In the Use task, listen for always and became.

peerObservation.focus: Identify the second sign (the shining hand), Moses’s mission and Harun’s support.
lookFor: Instruction: With your partner, fill the mission card: told to do, became, went with, why. Then mark six sentences I for instruction or E for event.
Check questions: How many parts on the card? (four) / What does I mean? (an instruction)
While learners work: Check the I and E marks by the first word of each sentence. Listen for “Who? Why?” in Activities 2–3. In the card swap, check that the other pair can explain the mission back.
Evidence of “Sign, mission, helper”: Names the sign, the mission and the helper.

reflectionLog: After each chapter, answer the chapter’s “After the lesson” question in one or two sentences.
Write down the rubric criterion that most learners had not yet reached and the support you gave.
Every three or four chapters, look at the grammar sequence of this book and plan one short recycling activity for a form learners still avoid.
Before the End-of-Level Test, read your notes and choose two chapters to revise with the class.
standardisation: Before scoring, read the A2 descriptors for written and spoken production in the CEFR table of this book.

With a colleague, score the same three writing papers on your own with the A2 writing bands (Task, Organisation, Grammar, Vocabulary). Then compare and talk about any criterion where your scores differ by more than one band.
Score one speaking test together in the same way: both listen, both score, then compare.
Keep one agreed paper for each band as a sample for later scoring.

selfAssessment.prompt: Chapter 3: Could learners do this by the end of the lesson: “Follow the chain problem → instructions → actions → feeling in the chapter”? Which stage of the lesson flow helped most, and which did not?
Chapter 5 is planned for 40 minutes. Which stage took longer than planned, and what did you move to the next lesson?
Before the pair or group work in Chapter 8, did you ask “How many strips?” How many learners could answer before they started?
In Chapter 16, how many learners were secure on “Final order of events”? What did you do for those who were not yet secure?

When you asked “What do people do on cold winter evenings in Türkiye (soba, tea, family visits)?” in Chapter 10, did learners describe other cultures with facts or with stereotypes? Which words did you give them?

Which of the likely errors listed for Chapter 12 did you hear (*Moses said him about Allah · *decided show · *can to do · *Then he puts (present in a past story))? Did you correct them during the activity or after it, and why?
Which app tools did your learners use with this book (audio, Word Notes, the exercises and their result codes)? Which one gave you the most useful information about their learning?
Read your reflection log for this book. What is one change you will make the next time you teach this book, and who will you share it with?

actionResearch.question: Do learners use must + base verb for a rule (Chapter 14) without adding to (*must to keep)?
steps: Baseline: in the Chapter 14 trip plan, count correct must sentences.
Recycle: in Chapters 15 and 16, ask for one rule with must for a safe class activity.
Check: after the A2 End-of-Level Test, note item 18 (must for obligation) for the class in Score a test.
Decide: compare the counts and decide whether learners need a contrast with have to (item 19).

collaboration: Share your counts for must for obligation with another English teacher who uses this book, and agree on one activity to try in both classes.
Plan the Chapter 14 trip plan (including a slower group member) with the physical education teacher for a real school walk.

objectives: I can say who Pharaoh was and who the Children of Israel were.
I can say why the king was rude to them.
I can use was, were and did not + verb.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Complete story sentences with was, were and believed. Fix two mistakes after did not: did not believe, did not think. Then build “Because of his fear, he was rude to the Children of Israel.” Remember: was for one person, were for more than one.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: MES-sen-ger, CRU-el, RU-ler, be-LIEVE. Say “the Children of Israel” as one group.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title and the picture. Who is the cruel king? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read the last four sentences again. What did the king fear? What did he do?
discussionPoints: The king was afraid, so he was unfair to a whole group. How can you be fair to a new person you do not know?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “Pharaoh” and “Children of Israel”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to the end of the chapter. Find “Because of his fear” and read the two sentences before it. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say three or four short sentences about new people, for example a new team or a new neighbor. Use was or were, believed or thought, did not + verb and because of.

whatToNotice: The chapter shows two sides: A cruel king and a big group who believed in one Allah.
Look at “He thought he was a god.” After thought, we hear the king’s idea. It was not true.
readListen: Look at the title and the picture. Who is the cruel king?
Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes.
Read the last four sentences again. What did the king fear? What did he do?
Tap the picture hotspots “Pharaoh” and “Children of Israel”.
findAnswerInStory: Start: Find two words that tell us what kind of ruler Pharaoh was.
Middle: Find who the Children of Israel were and what they believed.
End: Find the sentence that starts with “Because of his fear”.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: messenger, cruel, ruler, believe.
“He was an unfair and cruel ruler.” Was he kind to people? Say yes or no.
Write one sentence with believe, for example: I believe that …
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why the king was rude to the Children of Israel. Read the end of the chapter before you choose.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to the end of the chapter.
Find “Because of his fear” and read the two sentences before it.
Try again.
selfCheck: Can I say who Pharaoh was?
Can I say what the king feared?
Can I say “He did not believe …” correctly?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say three or four short sentences about new people, for example a new team or a new neighbor. Use was or were, believed or thought, did not + verb and because of.
content.reflectionPrompt: The king was afraid, so he was unfair to a whole group. How can you be fair to a new person you do not know?

objectives: I can tell the king’s dream and his order in the right order.
I can say what the magicians said about a boy.
I can use past verbs and will + verb.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Match past verbs with their base forms: had → have, saw → see, came → come, found → find, told → tell. Choose burnt and will. Then put five story sentences in order with One day, Then and When.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: des-POT-ic, ma-GI-cians, HEART-less. The -ed in searched sounds like /t/. Say “will be born” as one group.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title and the picture. What can you see in the fire? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read the chapter again and stop at One day, Then and When. What happens at each word?
discussionPoints: The king’s fear led to a very bad order. What can you do when fear makes you want to act fast?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “Fire in the Dream” and “A Cruel Order”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the chapter again from the start. Stop at One day, woke up, They said and Then. Put the events in that order. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say three short sentences about a safe, new situation, like a picnic day. Use will + verb for a prediction, one safe instruction, and When + past, past.

whatToNotice: A dream made the king afraid, and his fear led to a cruel order.
Look at “A boy will be born from the Children of Israel”. will talks about the future.
readListen: Look at the title and the picture. What can you see in the fire?
Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes.
Read the chapter again and stop at One day, Then and When. What happens at each word?
Tap the picture hotspots “Fire in the Dream” and “A Cruel Order”.
findAnswerInStory: Start: Find where the fire came from and what it burnt.
Middle: Find what the helpers and magicians said.
End: Find the king’s order to his soldiers and what the soldiers did.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: despotic, magicians, searched, heartless.
“They were unkind and heartless.” Did the soldiers feel sorry for the families?
Write one sentence with searched: I searched for my … everywhere.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will put four events in order. Follow the chapter from the first sentence to the last.
wrongAnswerSupport: Read the chapter again from the start.
Stop at One day, woke up, They said and Then.
Put the events in that order. Try again.
selfCheck: Can I say what the king saw in his dream?
Can I say what the magicians said?
Can I say one sentence with will + verb?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say three short sentences about a safe, new situation, like a picnic day. Use will + verb for a prediction, one safe instruction, and When + past, past.
content.reflectionPrompt: The king’s fear led to a very bad order. What can you do when fear makes you want to act fast?

content.chapter: Chapter 3: A Baby in a Basket
objectives: I can say why Moses’s mother was afraid.
I can say what Allah told her to do.
I can use could, could not and “told … to”.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Choose could or could not: Soldiers could find her baby, but she could not sleep. Complete lines with put, took and carried. Then fix two mistakes: told her daughter to follow, and kinder than (not more kind).
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: BAS-ket, pro-TECT, WOR-ried, FOL-low. The -ed in carried sounds like /d/.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title and the picture. Where is the baby? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read Allah’s words in quotation marks (“ ”) again. How many instructions can you find?
discussionPoints: Moses’s mother did a hard thing because she trusted Allah. Who helps you feel calm when you are worried?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “The Basket” and “The River Nile”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to the middle of the chapter. Find “Allah said to her” and read the words after it. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say three short sentences about a hard but safe moment, like a lost cat. Use could or could not, one instruction, will + verb and told … to.

whatToNotice: Moses’s mother was sad and worried, but she trusted Allah.
Look at “Allah was kinder to the baby Moses than she was.” kinder than compares two.
readListen: Look at the title and the picture. Where is the baby?
Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes.
Read Allah’s words in quotation marks (“ ”) again. How many instructions can you find?
Tap the picture hotspots “The Basket” and “The River Nile”.
findAnswerInStory: Start: Find why the mother could not sleep.
Middle: Find the four sentences Allah said to her.
End: Find who followed the basket.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: basket, protect, worried, follow.
“Allah will protect him.” Will the baby be safe or in danger?
Write one sentence with worried: I feel worried when …
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why the mother put her baby in the River Nile. Read the middle of the chapter, where Allah speaks to her.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to the middle of the chapter.
Find “Allah said to her” and read the words after it.
Try again.
selfCheck: Can I say why the mother could not sleep?
Can I say what the mother told her daughter?
Can I say “Allah was kinder … than …” correctly?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say three short sentences about a hard but safe moment, like a lost cat. Use could or could not, one instruction, will + verb and told … to.
content.reflectionPrompt: Moses’s mother did a hard thing because she trusted Allah. Who helps you feel calm when you are worried?

objectives: I can say who found the basket and what the queen decided.
I can say how the queen was different from the king.
I can use different from, I will and an order like Find ….
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Sort parts of the chapter: Going to a place (came to, took it to, ran to) or where something is (near, nearby). Match words like different from and accepted. Then choose I will take and Find a nurse.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: PAL-ace, SER-vants, kind-HEART-ed. Say the queen’s order in a clear voice: “Find a nurse for the baby.”
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title and the picture. Who is the queen? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read the words in quotation marks (“ ”) again. Who says each part?
discussionPoints: The queen and Moses’s sister helped a baby. What small help can you give to someone younger than you?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “Queen Asiye” and “The King’s Palace”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the chapter again, one person at a time. Start with “The palace servants” and end with “Moses’s sister saw everything.” Match again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four short sentences about a helpful person and a plan. Use be + adjective, different from, I will … and one safe order.

whatToNotice: Many people help baby Moses in this chapter: the servants, the queen and his sister.
Look at “The queen was different from her husband.” We say different from.
readListen: Look at the title and the picture. Who is the queen?
Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes.
Read the words in quotation marks (“ ”) again. Who says each part?
Tap the picture hotspots “Queen Asiye” and “The King’s Palace”.
findAnswerInStory: Start: Find where the basket came.
Middle: Find three words about the queen.
End: Find what Moses’s sister said to the queen.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: palace, servants, kind-hearted, nurse.
“She was good and kind-hearted.” Was the queen like her husband?
Write one sentence: My … is kind-hearted because …
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will match four people with what they did. Look for each person: the servants, the queen, the king and Moses’s sister.
wrongAnswerSupport: Read the chapter again, one person at a time.
Start with “The palace servants” and end with “Moses’s sister saw everything.”
Match again.
selfCheck: Can I say who took the basket to the king and the queen?
Can I say one way the queen was different from the king?
Can I say “I will …” to make a decision?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four short sentences about a helpful person and a plan. Use be + adjective, different from, I will … and one safe order.
content.reflectionPrompt: The queen and Moses’s sister helped a baby. What small help can you give to someone younger than you?

objectives: I can say how Allah sent Moses back to his mother.
I can say why Moses loved the Children of Israel.
I can use always, because and was walking.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Match words like take care of, grew up and became with their meanings. Complete lines with always and because. Then decide: Was Moses walking first, or did he see the men first?
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: ba-ZAAR, al-WAYS, be-CAUSE. Say “take care of” and “grew up” as one group each.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title and the picture. Who is holding the baby? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read the last three sentences again. What did Moses see?
discussionPoints: Moses was always ready to help the weak people. Who needs a little help in your home or class?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “His Mother’s Arms” and “The Bazaar”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to the middle of the chapter. Find “He loved the Children of Israel” and read to the end of that sentence. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say three or four short sentences about someone who helps others. Use look after or take care of, became, always and because.

whatToNotice: Moses grew up in the king’s house, but he always loved Allah.
Look at “One day he was walking in the bazaar. He saw two men. They were fighting.” He was walking, and then he saw.
readListen: Look at the title and the picture. Who is holding the baby?
Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes.
Read the last three sentences again. What did Moses see?
Tap the picture hotspots “His Mother’s Arms” and “The Bazaar”.
findAnswerInStory: Start: Find who brought the mother to the palace.
Middle: Find two things that were always true about Moses.
End: Find where Moses was walking one day.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: take care of, safe, grew up, weak.
“He was always ready to help the weak people.” Did Moses help strong people or weak people?
Write one sentence: I grew up in …
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why Moses loved the Children of Israel. Read the middle of the chapter and look for the word because.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to the middle of the chapter.
Find “He loved the Children of Israel” and read to the end of that sentence.
Try again.
selfCheck: Can I say who looked after baby Moses?
Can I say why Moses loved the Children of Israel?
Can I use was walking and saw in one short story?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say three or four short sentences about someone who helps others. Use look after or take care of, became, always and because.
content.reflectionPrompt: Moses was always ready to help the weak people. Who needs a little help in your home or class?

content.chapter: Chapter 6: A Mistake in the Bazaar
objectives: I can say what happened in the bazaar.
I can say how Moses felt and what he asked Allah.
I can use to + verb, because and are going to.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Choose what accidentally means. Choose to help and because: Ran to help him, forgave him because He is Kind and Loving. Then fix a friend’s warning: Are looking for you, are going to catch you.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: ac-ci-DEN-tal-ly, up-SET, for-GAVE. Say “Help me!” loudly, and say the dua calmly.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title and the picture. What mistake happened? Listen to the chapter once. This chapter is sad, so take your time. Read the man’s warning at the end again. What must Moses do?
discussionPoints: Moses made a mistake, felt sorry and asked Allah to forgive him. What can you do after you make a mistake?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “Not on Purpose” and “The Warning”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to the middle of the chapter. Find the word accidentally and read that sentence again. Ask yourself: Did Moses plan it? Then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four short sentences with a safe warning, like a wet floor at school. Use to + verb, because, are + -ing, are going to and one order.

whatToNotice: Moses wanted to help, but a man died. Moses was very sorry.
Look at “Moses ran to help him.” to help tells us why he ran.
readListen: Look at the title and the picture. What mistake happened?
Listen to the chapter once. This chapter is sad, so take your time.
Read the man’s warning at the end again. What must Moses do?
Tap the picture hotspots “Not on Purpose” and “The Warning”.
findAnswerInStory: Start: Find what the weak man shouted.
Middle: Find Moses’s dua to Allah.
End: Find what the king’s soldiers are going to do.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: shouted, upset, accidentally, forgave.
“Moses was very upset.” Was he happy or sad?
Write one sentence with accidentally: I accidentally dropped my …
content.quickChallengeGuide: The sentence is about how the death happened. Read the middle of the chapter before you decide.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to the middle of the chapter.
Find the word accidentally and read that sentence again.
Ask yourself: Did Moses plan it? Then try again.
selfCheck: Can I say why Moses ran to the two men?
Can I say what Moses asked Allah?
Can I say “they are going to …” correctly?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four short sentences with a safe warning, like a wet floor at school. Use to + verb, because, are + -ing, are going to and one order.
content.reflectionPrompt: Moses made a mistake, felt sorry and asked Allah to forgive him. What can you do after you make a mistake?

objectives: I can say why Moses left Egypt.
I can say what Moses saw at the well.
I can use there were, were + -ing and arrived at.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Choose was or were for the people at the well: There were, They were watering, Two girls were sitting. Complete arrived at, So and looked for. Then match journey words like escaped from and shepherds.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: es-CAPED, GUI-ded, THIRS-ty, SHEP-herds. The -ed in guided is an extra part, but the -ed in escaped sounds like /t/.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title and the picture. Where is Moses going? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read the sentences about the well again. Who is near the water? Who is far?
discussionPoints: Moses was tired and far from home, but he was not alone. Who helps you when you are in a new place?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “Midian” and “The Well”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to the middle of the chapter. Find “Midian was near Egypt.” and read the next sentence too. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four short sentences about a safe trip. Use After …, arrived at, so, looked for, there were and was or were + -ing.

whatToNotice: Moses was alone on the road, but the story says Allah guided him.
Look at “Two girls were sitting far from the water.” were sitting shows what they were doing at that moment.
readListen: Look at the title and the picture. Where is Moses going?
Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes.
Read the sentences about the well again. Who is near the water? Who is far?
Tap the picture hotspots “Midian” and “The Well”.
findAnswerInStory: Start: Find why Moses escaped.
Middle: Find two sentences about Midian.
End: Find Moses’s question to the girls.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: escaped, guided, thirsty, well.
“Moses was tired and thirsty.” What did he need?
Write one sentence: I am thirsty, so I …
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why Midian was a safe place. Read the sentences about Midian in the middle of the chapter.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to the middle of the chapter.
Find “Midian was near Egypt.” and read the next sentence too.
Try again.
selfCheck: Can I say why Moses left Egypt?
Can I say who was at the well?
Can I say “There were many …” correctly?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four short sentences about a safe trip. Use After …, arrived at, so, looked for, there were and was or were + -ing.
content.reflectionPrompt: Moses was tired and far from home, but he was not alone. Who helps you when you are in a new place?

objectives: I can say why the two sisters waited at the well.
I can say how Moses helped them.
I can ask a question with Why aren’t you …?
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Choose what cannot come means. Build Moses’s question “Why aren’t you taking your sheep to drink water?” Then fix the sisters’ words: There are no young men, and wait for the other shepherds to leave.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: un-der-STOOD, EAR-ly, SHEP-herds. Let your voice go down at the end of “Why aren’t you taking your sheep to drink water?”
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title and the picture. What are the sisters doing? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read the sisters’ words again. Why do they wait?
discussionPoints: Moses saw that the sisters needed help, and he helped them. How can you see when a friend needs help?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “Waiting for Their Turn” and “Water for the Sheep”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the chapter again from the start. Stop after the girls speak, after Moses helps, and after they go home. Put the events in that order. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four short sentences about a shared job at home. Use Why aren’t you …?, cannot, There are no …, so and wait for.

whatToNotice: The sisters had a problem, and Moses understood it quickly.
Look at “He cannot come with us.” cannot means he is not able.
readListen: Look at the title and the picture. What are the sisters doing?
Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes.
Read the sisters’ words again. Why do they wait?
Tap the picture hotspots “Waiting for Their Turn” and “Water for the Sheep”.
findAnswerInStory: Start: Find Moses’s question.
Middle: Find the girls’ answer and why they wait for their turn.
End: Find what the father asked and what the sisters said.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: turn, understood, early, shepherds.
“We wait for our turn.” Do the sisters go first or last?
Write one sentence: I came home early because …
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will put four events in order. Follow the chapter from the well to the sisters’ home.
wrongAnswerSupport: Read the chapter again from the start.
Stop after the girls speak, after Moses helps, and after they go home.
Put the events in that order. Try again.
selfCheck: Can I say why the father did not come?
Can I say what Moses did for the sisters?
Can I ask “Why aren’t you …?” correctly?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four short sentences about a shared job at home. Use Why aren’t you …?, cannot, There are no …, so and wait for.
content.reflectionPrompt: Moses saw that the sisters needed help, and he helped them. How can you see when a friend needs help?

objectives: I can say who the sisters’ father was.
I can say why Moses accepted the job.
I can use want to, decided to and because.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Complete lines with couldn’t, because and needed. Choose to thank and to go after want and decided. Then put four sentences in order with Later and After ten years.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: OF-fered, ac-CEP-ted, STRAN-ger, MAR-ried. The -ed in accepted is an extra part.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title and the picture. Where does Moses live now? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read the last four sentences again. How long did Moses stay?
discussionPoints: Shu’ayb (pbuh) wanted to thank Moses for his work. How can you thank someone who helped you?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “Prophet Shu’ayb” and “A Home in Midian”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to the middle of the chapter. Find “Moses accepted the job” and read to the end of the next sentence. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four short sentences about a new chance, like a new club. Use need, because, want to, offer or accept, later and decided to.

whatToNotice: A kind act at the well gave Moses a new home and a new family.
Look at Later and “After ten years”. These words move the story forward in time.
readListen: Look at the title and the picture. Where does Moses live now?
Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes.
Read the last four sentences again. How long did Moses stay?
Tap the picture hotspots “Prophet Shu’ayb” and “A Home in Midian”.
findAnswerInStory: Start: Find who the father was and why he couldn’t help his daughters.
Middle: Find what Shu’ayb (pbuh) offered Moses.
End: Find what Moses decided after ten years.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: offered, accepted, stranger, married.
“he was a stranger in Midian”: Did people in Midian know Moses?
Write one sentence: My friend offered me …
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why Moses accepted Shu’ayb’s (pbuh) offer. Read the middle of the chapter before you choose.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to the middle of the chapter.
Find “Moses accepted the job” and read to the end of the next sentence.
Try again.
selfCheck: Can I say who Shu’ayb (pbuh) was?
Can I say two things Moses needed?
Can I say “I want to …” correctly?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four short sentences about a new chance, like a new club. Use need, because, want to, offer or accept, later and decided to.
content.reflectionPrompt: Shu’ayb (pbuh) wanted to thank Moses for his work. How can you thank someone who helped you?

content.chapter: Chapter 10: The Voice on the Mountain
objectives: I can describe the cold, dark night in the valley.
I can say what Allah told Moses on the mountain.
I can use It was, There was and to + verb.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Choose It or There: It was winter, There was nobody on the way, It was getting dark. Build Moses’s words “Wait here. I will get some fire to get warm.” Then match words like valley, Suddenly and turned into.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: HILL-side, SI-lence, SUD-den-ly. Say “walking stick” with the stress on WALK.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title and the picture. What is on the hillside? Listen to the chapter once. Listen well for the voice in the silence. Read the last three sentences again. What happened to the walking stick?
discussionPoints: Moses went to get fire to keep his family warm. What do you do to take care of your family?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “Fire on the Hillside” and “The Walking Stick”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to the middle of the chapter. Find “Wait here.” and read Moses’s next words. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four short sentences about a cold evening. Use getting + adjective, there is or there are, one instruction, I will … and to + verb.

whatToNotice: The night was dark, cold and very quiet. Then Moses heard a loud voice.
Look at “It was getting dark and cold.” getting shows a slow change.

metadata.title: Moses A2 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Look • Listen • Read • Check • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 20 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: A2 learners who study the story of Prophet Moses (pbuh) at home or on their own.
learningGoals: Understand the 16 chapters of the story of Moses (pbuh).
Find the answer sentence in the story.
Learn the Word Notes of each chapter.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
Turn trust, helping and fairness into small actions.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Answer the Quick Challenge before you read the feedback.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 16.

sections.title: 1. One Chapter at a Time
sections.text: Study one chapter in one sitting. It takes about 20 minutes. Open “Study Path” to see the steps for your chapter.
points: Look at the title and the picture.
Listen and follow the text.
Read a few sentences at a time.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 2. Listen and Read
sections.text: Every chapter has audio. Listen first, then read.
points: First time: Listen for the main idea.
Second time: Follow the words with your eyes.
Stop the audio and say one short sentence again.

sections.title: 3. Word Notes and Hotspots
sections.text: Each chapter has four underlined words. Tap a word to see its Word Note. Tap the hotspots on the picture for short notes.
points: Read the word in its sentence first.
Guess the meaning, then check the Word Note.
Write the word and one sentence in your notebook.

sections.title: 4. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Each chapter has one Quick Challenge. Answer first, then read the feedback.
points: Wrong answer? Find the answer sentence.
Read it again.
Try again.

sections.title: 5. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has four Language Focus activities. Do them after you understand the chapter. They use sentences from the story.
points: Activity 1: look at a story sentence and its meaning.
Activities 2 and 3: practise the words and forms.
Last activity: Write or say three or four sentences of your own.

sections.title: 6. When It Is Hard
sections.text: It is fine to find a chapter hard. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Listen to half of the chapter only.
Read two or three sentences at a time.
Look at the picture and the hotspots again.
Learn only two words today.

sections.title: 7. Values in the Story
sections.text: The story of Moses (pbuh) is about trust in Allah, saying sorry, helping, thanks and fairness. Turn each value into one small action.
points: Trust: Moses’s mother trusted Allah when she was worried (Chapter 3).
Saying sorry: Say sorry and ask Allah to forgive you after a mistake (Chapter 6).
Helping: Help people who cannot do a job alone (Chapter 8).
Thanks: Thank people who help you (Chapter 9).
Calm: Stay calm and help scared people (Chapter 15).
Fairness: No one can own another person (Chapters 1 and 16).

sections.title: 8. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 16, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Knowledge Check
